detail.abstract: Prior authorization (PA) requires clinicians to obtain payer approval before delivering covered services. In outpatient physical therapy (PT), authorizations are typically granted for a limited number of visits within a fixed date window, so a single episode of care can require several requests, extensions and appeals. A 2025 American Physical Therapy Association survey of 856 respondents found that 30.2% waited one to two weeks for PA decisions, up from 20.9% in 2018, and that nearly 83% agreed PA had caused patients to abandon treatment. Independent practices, the large majority of an estimated 39,000 US outpatient PT clinics, absorb this burden with few administrative staff and little information technology. This paper describes how PA works in outpatient PT, summarizes published evidence of its burden, explains why small practices are disproportionately affected, and reviews the policy landscape, including the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), which sets decision timeframes from January 2026 and requires payer PA application programming interfaces by January 2027, and a voluntary June 2025 pledge by health plans covering 257 million people. It closes with recommendations for practices, payers and technology developers, and a research agenda.

detail.abstract: We examine how sectoral complementarity and geopolitical alignment jointly shape greenfield foreign direct investment (FDI) to Latin America. Using a novel project-level database of greenfield investment from 2003–2024, combined with a bilateral geopolitical distance index and sector-level revealed comparative advantage measures, we show how geopolitical distance affects the volume and sectoral allocation of FDI, and how this effect interacts with underlying competitiveness. We find that greater geopolitical distance significantly reduces greenfield FDI to Latin America, with the impact becoming more pronounced since the mid-2010s across major FDI source countries. While sectoral complementarity between source and destination countries remains an important positive determinant of FDI, its effect weakens as geopolitical tension rises. The impact of geopolitical distance is particularly strong in high-tech manufacturing, transportation, and ICT sectors. We also show that bilateral investment treaties and free trade agreements can help moderate the effects of geopolitical distance on FDI. The findings highlight the importance of diversifying investment sources in an increasingly complex global environment and underscore the critical role of robust investment and trade agreements in mitigating policy uncertainty.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Aggregate Labor Productivity: Evidence from Patent Data

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the aggregate impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology on labor productivity, exploiting patent data in OECD countries during 2000-2017. We first document that after accelerating in 2000, the issuance of AI technology related patents has more than tripled by 2017 and OECD countries held about 89 percent of all these patents across the world during the same period. Second, using a production function approach, we find that considering the pace of AI patent applications over the 2000-2017, labor productivity, measured as output per worker, has consequently increased by between 0.8 percent to 1.2 percent. The estimates also imply that innovation in AI technology could raise aggregate labor productivity by up to 3.8 percent in the long-run. These suggest that productivity gains could be larger in the future as the pace of innovation in AI gains new speed and spread to more sectors of the economy. These results are robust to accounting for a proxy of AI technology spillovers from other countries.  Further we find that countries with a high share of employees in professional and managerial roles benefit from larger labor productivity gains  and AI technology. Furthermore, these gains from task complementarity may take time to materialize as workers learn to fully appropriate the technology. Finally, labor market flexibility could also play a role in shaping labor productivity gains by enabling workers mobility.

detail.abstract: During an expanding epidemic, cumulative cases, deaths, and recoveries do not form a contemporaneously closed ledger because recent cases remain outcome-censored and terminal outcomes can enter surveillance through different pathways. We reconstructed national outcome accounting across 86 official situation reports from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The unresolved stock, defined as confirmed cases minus confirmed deaths and recorded recoveries, increased from 107 cases on May 27 to 2,022 on September 13, while its proportion declined from 85.6% to 27.9%. Using an oldest-outcomes-first allocation, at least 864 cases from the cumulative population reported 14 days earlier and 278 from that reported approximately 3 weeks earlier could not be represented among terminal outcomes by September 13. The crude residual is therefore not a count of missing outcomes, but age-stratified closure can reveal a smaller reconciliation backlog concealed by cumulative indicators.

detail.abstract: Reported case-fatality ratios (CFRs) during active Ebola outbreaks reflect surveillance processes as well as disease biology. During the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, North Kivu repeatedly reported a substantially higher cumulative confirmed-case CFR than Ituri. We reconstructed the complete available national SitRep sequence through 13 September 2026. The primary estimand was the proportion of newly laboratory-positive persons already deceased when reported positive. We used matched-SitRep comparisons, a Mantel-Haenszel analysis, a Bayesian binomial logistic model with province-by-reporting-regime interaction, postmortem-surveillance triangulation, counterfactual standardization, and pre-specified influence analyses. Missing fields were not imputed. Twenty-eight matched SitReps contained compatible living/deceased laboratory-positive splits. Across these reports, 415/1,507 (27.5%) classified positives in Ituri and 265/568 (46.7%) in North Kivu were already deceased when reported positive (Mantel-Haenszel OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.76-2.70). Bayesian estimates showed a modest early contrast but a substantial late contrast: 27.6% (95% CrI 24.8-30.5) in Ituri versus 48.6% (44.2-53.1) in North Kivu during SitReps 96-122. Counterfactual calculations showed that ascertainment differences of this magnitude could reproduce most of the observed cumulative CFR contrast. North Kivu's higher reported CFR was accompanied by substantially more confirmation after death. Differential ascertainment is therefore a central component of the observed geographic fatality heterogeneity, although aggregate SitReps cannot determine how much residual difference reflects biological severity, delayed presentation, treatment access, care capacity, or remaining measurement bias.

title: Generative AI and the Limits of Productivity Measurement in the System of National Accounts
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Generative AI and the Limits of Productivity Measurement in the System of National Accounts

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract:
In 1987, Robert Solow famously remarked that the computer age was visible everywhere except in the productivity statistics (Solow 1987). Nearly four decades later, the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) raises related questions about whether official statistics adequately capture the productivity effects of a new general-purpose technology. Micro-level evidence points to substantial efficiency gains in a wide range of cognitive and service-oriented tasks: experimental and field studies report productivity improvements of 14 to 56 percent across customer support, professional writing, software development, consulting, and legal analysis (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond 2025; Noy and Zhang 2023; Peng and others 2023; Dell’Acqua and others 2023; Choi, Monahan, and Schwarcz 2024). Recent aggregate data are also more encouraging than they appeared a year ago: average labor productivity growth across the OECD doubled to 1.2 percent in 2024, with the United States standing out at +2.2 percent, while the euro area remained close to zero (OECD 2026a). The OECD itself interprets these developments as possibly providing “early, tentative signals consistent with a productivity-enhancing role of AI” (OECD 2026a, p. 11). Even so, the magnitude of measured aggregate gains remains modest relative to the emerging micro evidence, and several structural features of the statistical framework continue to limit how much of the underlying improvement can be captured.
This paper argues that two features of the System of National Accounts (SNA) constrain the measurement of productivity gains from generative AI. First, a significant share of the sectors most exposed to AI— particularly public administration, education, and health—rely on non-market output measurement, where output is valued using a sum-of-costs approach (United Nations and others 2009; United Nations and others 2025). Under this framework, output is by construction closely tied to inputs, implying that measured productivity growth is constrained even when underlying efficiency improves (Atkinson 2005; Schreyer 2010). Second, in market-based service sectors, the absence of adequate quality adjustment in price indices can result in improvements in service quality—such as faster delivery, greater accuracy, or expanded functionality—being insufficiently captured in real output measures (Triplett and Bosworth 2004; Byrne, Fernald, and Reinsdorf 2016; Syverson 2017). These features do not preclude the measurement of AI-driven gains entirely—and the 2024 data suggest that some gains are now being picked up in countries where AI investment has been concentrated—but they imply that the share of true productivity improvement reflected in official statistics is likely to remain incomplete, particularly in service-heavy economies.
The paper contributes to the literature by (i) linking the sectoral incidence of generative AI to known measurement challenges in the national accounts, drawing on recent task-based exposure studies (Eloundou and others 2024; Cazzaniga and others 2024; OECD 2026b, Box 1.1); (ii) providing an accounting framework that clarifies how non-market output measures and unadjusted service prices dampen measured productivity growth; (iii) assessing whether the inclusion of a return to capital in non-market output—as recommended in the 2025 SNA—can mitigate this gap; and (iv) outlining potential avenues for improvement, including outcome based volume indicators, enhanced quality adjustment in service price indices, and exogenous multifactor productivity adjustments applied through the deflator. The findings have important implications for policy: if AI related productivity gains are even partially underestimated, assessments of economic performance and potential output may be biased downward (Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson 2021). Broader welfare gains may also be missed unless supplemented by measures outside the core national accounts.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the drivers of domestic revenue mobilization in emerging and developing economies (EMDEs) vary across levels of revenue performance, with a particular focus on non resource tax. Using panel quantile regressions for 118 countries over 1990-2022, we find substantial heterogeneity in the correlates of revenue mobilization. At relatively low tax performance, after accounting for country-fixed effects, per capita income growth, IMF technical assistance, and governance quality are most strongly associated with revenue gains. By contrast, at relatively higher tax-to-GDP level, governance quality appears to be the most robust correlate. Focusing on the role of technical assistance, we construct a novel shift-share instrument by interacting annual aggregate IMF capacity-development resources with a predetermined measure of country exposure. Our IV-based analysis supports the idea that technical assistance matters most when tax performance is relatively low. These results highlight the need to tailor reform strategies, with focused technical assistance where revenue performance is relatively low, while strengthening the role of governance and the social contract in sustaining high levels of domestic revenue mobilization.

detail.abstract: Social insurance often relies on third-party gatekeepers to certify eligibility, but planners cannot easily verify whether those certifications are accurate. We study this problem in the market for medical sick leave using the universe of sick leave certificates in Chile from 2018-2022 (about 22 million records). We estimate how a sharp increase in enforcement changes behavior on both the supply side (physicians) and the demand side (workers). We combine matched difference-indifferences and regression discontinuity in time on physicians, and a design that addresses non-random patient exposure. Enforcement produces a large and persistent drop in issuance among the highest-issuing physicians, with smaller spillovers to similar non-sanctioned physicians. Workers who were more exposed to these physicians reduce sick-leave use, but the final effects are smaller than the supply contraction, consistent with imperfect substitution on the worker side across providers. Workplace networks strengthen these effects, suggesting that information and access to substitute certifiers are channeled through coworkers. The findings show how substitution and spillovers shape the ultimate impact of monitoring policies.

detail.abstract: When a language model restates a published statistic, the number usually survives and the sentence around it usually does not: the population, period, program scope and permitted inference are dropped or replaced. This failure is filed under "hallucination", which places it entirely on the model. This paper moves half of it back to the publisher. It specifies Claim Contract 1.0, a small machine-readable format in which a statistic ships with the conditions under which it may be restated; a reference implementation covering 189 claims from the 2025 federal HMDA record (1,187,606 FHA credit decisions); a publisher-agnostic checker; and a runnable fidelity task that grades an answer twice, for value and for fidelity to the contract, under four conditions of source access. On one model, 12 questions × 3 repeats per condition, a contract-shaped sentence in the tool output did not change value correctness (27/27) or full-credit answers (11/36 and 11/36) but changed the mix of failures toward copying past the contracted edge rather than inventing. A verification token (claim receipt) embedded in prose survived in 0/36 answers; a receipt-aware client carried it in 23/36 at full coverage and still forged two. Receipts now carry an issue channel, the publisher's claim snapshot is signed and recorded in a public transparency log, and the figures are recomputed from the CFPB file in an attested build. Auditing the publisher's own pages during the experiment found thirteen error families; the model was faithful and the publisher was wrong, and every fidelity figure is bounded accordingly. Observed results are sensitive to evaluation configuration; the study cannot separate model behaviour from grader and prompt-condition effects. Nothing here is a finding about language models in general.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the processes of administrative, fiscal, and political decentralization in Cuba following the 2019 constitutional reforms. Despite legislative changes aimed at enhancing municipal autonomy, the study argues that decentralization efforts have fallen short of devolving significant power to local governments. Drawing on Falleti's (2010) sequential theory of decentralization and Rondinelli's (1981) degrees of decentralization, the analysis reveals that Cuba's decentralization is predominantly characterized by deconcentration and delegation, with limited instances of true devolution. The paper highlights the persistent influence of the national government over local decision-making, particularly in fiscal and administrative domains, and explores the implications of these constraints for territorial development. Through an exploratory case study, the study assesses the regulatory framework and its impact on local governance, emphasizing the need for greater political decentralization and citizen participation to achieve meaningful autonomy. The findings suggest that without substantial devolution of power, Cuba's decentralization efforts risk remaining symbolic rather than transformative.

title: The Memory-augmented Rough SABR Filter: Exact Markovian Lifts for Sequential Inference of Rough Volatility from Option Panels

detail.title: The Memory-augmented Rough SABR Filter: Exact Markovian Lifts for Sequential Inference of Rough Volatility from Option Panels

detail.abstract: We study sequential inference for a rough SABR model whose log-volatility is driven by a Riemann-Liouville fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index H ∈ (0, 1 2) and which is observed only through noisy panels of option quotes. Because the driver is not Markov, the exact filtering state is a path. We replace the fractional kernel by an exponential sum obtained from a generalised Gauss-Laguerre quadrature of its Laplace representation, which lifts the driver to finitely many Ornstein-Uhlenbeck memory factors and makes the augmented state Markov. We prove that, within the lifted model, the memory transition, the leverage coupling between the forward shock and the memory increments, and the exponential martingale normalisation of volatility are all exact; we give a closed-form meansquare bound for the distance between the lifted and the exact volatility in terms of the L 2 kernel error, and we prove convergence of option prices as the lift is refined when β = 1. We also show that the lifted driver is a semimartingale whose small-scale behaviour is Brownian with an explicit amplification constant, that a right-point discretisation of the pricing map induces a non-vanishing drift of order ρν, and that the plug-in Monte Carlo likelihood is, in expectation, an exact Gaussian likelihood with inflated variance. The resulting particle filter is applied to 1,600 five-minute panels of Deribit bitcoin options against a matched Markovian SABR benchmark. The lifted filter attains higher one-step-ahead predictive scores in each of four non-overlapping windows and over five paired seeds, with lower price errors and better-calibrated predictive intervals. Our theory identifies which features of the lift can and cannot be credited for this gain.

with automatic differentiation, and what this costs in accuracy. The network is positive, con-

against per-slice SVI, SSVI, a soft-penalty MLP, and a Dugas-style ablation, on clean data and

convexity, Durrleman, and calendar violations in all 15 runs (tolerance 10⁻⁴). The soft penalty

and per-slice SVI shows 2.69–3.88% Durrleman and 17.86–31.02% calendar violations. The

detail.abstract: Why do some conflicts end in exhaustion, some persist indefinitely, and some reignite more easily than they began? This paper shows that a single underlying game, in which actors dispute a contested object under incomplete information, can generate all three. Three features classify conflict form: whether some actors gain a non-material reward only by participating in escalation, whether the object is ordinary or scarce, and whether escalation capacity runs out within the conflict's horizon. Together they define eight regions, each with its own available mechanisms; threshold events, damage, and resource depletion then determine how far those mechanisms develop. Participation-contingent commitment departs most sharply from resolve-signaling models: it opens a window in which committed actors escalate while strategic actors hold back, so escalation reveals type. The architecture implies that renewed conflict can begin below original onset, that revealing commitment can make conflict networks more fragile, and that conflicts become hardest to read just when they are hardest to settle.

detail.abstract: Do early investments in parents pay off even when treatment effects for children appear to fade out quickly? We answer this question by leveraging a field experiment in which households with 3-5 year-old children were randomized into a parenting program, a preschool, or a control group, combined with a natural experiment (Covid-19 school closures) that occurred ten years later. Prior to the closures, treatment effects on academic achievement had faded to zero across all groups. Yet, with Covid-19 school closures, effects of the parenting program re-emerge: test scores in control and preschool groups drop by roughly 0.25-0.30 SD, whereas scores in the parenting group drop by only 0.11 SD (difference: p = 0.01). Our findings suggest that parenting programs can generate latent human capital that only becomes visible when complementary school inputs are removed. This result is consonant with parental and school investments acting as substitutes in skill production. Because this latent parental capacity pays off precisely when school inputs fail, standard measurement tools for early childhood programs can miss crucial state-contingent value.

detail.abstract: Nigeria faces one of the world's most severe foundational learning crises, where schooling does not consistently translate to learning. With an estimated 10.5 million children out of school and 70% of primary pupils unable to read or perform basic arithmetic by age ten (UNICEF, 2022; World Bank & UNESCO, 2022), the nation's ambition to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) quality and inclusive education for all remains under threat. In this context, Low-Fee Private Schools (LFPSs) have emerged as indispensable yet under-recognized community-based actors providing affordable education in low-income, peri-urban, and rural settlements where public systems are either absent or overstretched. This study, conducted under the All Hands on Deck for SDG 4 (AHOD) initiative in Gwagwalada Area Council, Federal Capital Territory, investigates the role of LFPSs in bridging Nigeria's foundational learning divide. It employs a mixed-method design, integrating primary data from 18 LFPSs with secondary national and global datasets from UBEC, UNESCO, UNICEF, and the World Bank. Descriptive and comparative analyses reveal that while 94% of sampled schools have engaged with government authorities; but engagement is mostly transactional, focused on licensing, inspection, or ad-hoc training. Collaboration quality is poor; only 11% described it as strong." Key constraints include financial fragility (78%), information asymmetry (67%), and bureaucratic barriers (50%). Nonetheless, 100% of schools expressed willingness to partner with government, and 94% identified professional training and capacity development as urgent priorities. Findings confirm that LFPSs contribute significantly to access and learning equity, serving approximately 23% of Nigeria's primary school population and 60% of children in low-income communities. Yet, systemic neglect in policy inclusion, funding, and teacher professionalization threatens their sustainability. The paper argues that LFPSs are not marginal players but strategic partners in achieving equitable education. It recommends a national LFPS integration framework, micro-grant financing mechanisms, continuous professional development (CPD) pathways, and Education Management Information System (EMIS) inclusion. By harnessing the collective strength of state and non-state actors, Nigeria can transform LFPSs from invisible providers into recognized drivers of equity, inclusion, and foundational learning, advancing progress toward SDG 4.

detail.abstract: Mathematics is characterized by abstract objects of study that cannot always be directly observed, requiring learners to engage in abstraction and higher-order thinking. This abstract nature often becomes a source of difficulty, particularly for students at the concrete operational stage of cognitive development. Difficulties in understanding concepts and symbols, connecting mathematical ideas to real-world situations, and developing reasoning and problem-solving abilities may contribute to mathematics anxiety-a psychological condition marked by tension, apprehension, and fear when engaging with mathematical tasks. This study presents a literature-based examination of mathematics anxiety and its impact on learning outcomes. The discussion elaborates the characteristics of abstract mathematics, including its symbolic and representational nature, the necessity of abstraction, and the importance of bridging concrete experiences with abstract concepts. It identifies common problems encountered by students, such as grasping conceptual meaning, interpreting symbols, relating concepts to everyday contexts, and applying reasoning and problem-solving strategies. Internal factors (interest, motivation, attention, readiness, and physical condition), external factors (family, school, social environment, and learning facilities), and teacher-related factors (pedagogical competence, instructional methods, media selection, and evaluation) are examined as contributors to learning difficulties that may exacerbate mathematics anxiety. The study also explores pedagogical approaches to alleviate such anxiety, including concrete media and manipulatives, technology-based and visual learning, and active, contextual, and meaningful learning. The findings suggest that mathematics anxiety is closely linked to the abstract nature of mathematics and classroom instructional practices, and that appropriate pedagogical interventions can mitigate its adverse effects on students' mathematics learning outcomes.

detail.abstract: An instrument can leave the conditional mean of an endogenous regressor unchanged while shifting its distribution. We develop inference for this distributional first stage by inverting a residual-independence test in a constant-coefficient model. Under a known assignment symmetry, the confidence set has finite-sample coverage regardless of relevance strength or disturbance moments. Constructive identification results show how full independence recovers information missed by every prespecified residual-power order. The first nonzero derivative of residual dependence determines the local coefficient scale n-1/(2r) and a Gaussian squared-norm power function; an oracle comparison quantifies the cost of an unknown dependence direction. For independent bounded-size cells, an unbiased score detects distributional signals above a √ S boundary, with a matching least-favorable lower bound over unknown cell directions. Simulations assess these rates and compare mean-based, targeted, and omnibus procedures. Within the same exact framework, features matched to a known channel gain power, while a prespecified second-moment-HSIC hybrid reduces relative worst-power losses across the simulated channel menu. A quarter-of-birth stress test illustrates additional model restrictions detected by distributional scores under matched aggregation.

detail.abstract: Quantile-parameterized distributions (QPDs) provide flexible continuous representations of elicited or empirical probability-quantile pairs. Flexible QPD families, including Metalog and QFlex, can achieve highly accurate fits but may also introduce distributional features not supported by the underlying population. We study this structural overfitting, focusing on the number, location, and stability of fitted modes. Using Johnson distributions as known populations, we employ Monte Carlo simulation and bootstrap resampling to distinguish population features from those induced by sampling variation and model flexibility, and then examine three empirical datasets. We find that higher-order QPDs can produce spurious modes even as quantile-space fit improves, may require large samples for structural stability, and can yield mode locations and heights that remain highly sensitive to sampling variation. QFlex coefficient restrictions provide additional control over modality and generally reduce, but do not eliminate, this behavior. These results demonstrate that improved fit to empirical quantiles does not necessarily imply more reliable density structure. We recommend that modes inferred from flexible QPDs be supported by statistical evidence and stability analysis, and that structural constraints, such as those provided by QFlex, be used when appropriate to regularize modality.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of policy responses to the 2026 energy shock using the newly constructed IMF Global Policy Tracker. The main analysis focuses on measures announced between end-February and early June, while preliminary data through mid-September shed light on how policy responses evolved as energy prices began to normalize. The findings point to distinct drivers of policy composition and design. At average public debt levels, greater shock exposure is associated with a larger share of price pass-through measures. As debt rises, this association strengthens, while the relationship between exposure and fiscal shielding weakens. Monetary responses are driven mainly by pre-shock inflation developments, while financial-stabilization measures are more closely associated with reserve adequacy. Policy design—including targeting and temporariness—is shaped more by institutional capacity, inflation, and the political cycle than by shock exposure. The extended dataset shows a gradual shift away from fiscal shielding toward pass-through, demand- and inflation- management measures. Later announcements are more likely to identify beneficiaries but less likely to include explicit expiry dates or sunset provisions. The main findings broadly hold, although some become less statistically significant.

detail.abstract: Market-based policies for emissions reduction, including emissions trading systems, have been adopted or considered by many regions. How to cover emissions from energy-intensive trade-exposed (EITE) sectors under these or other systems has long been debated due to the potential negative impacts on industrial competitiveness and emissions leakage. A common perception is that pursuing climate objectives would harm EITE industries, while trade or industrial policies would serve purposes unrelated to emissions reduction. However, in regions and sectors in which production is cleaner, on average, than production of major trading partners, it may be possible to combine climate and trade measures to support both emissions reduction and industrial competitiveness, while also limiting price impacts. We explore this question by comparing different emissions reduction policy instruments for U.S. steelmaking that include both domestic and border policy components. We also vary coverage assumptions for the same instrument, comparing a coupled policy to either a domestic or border policy alone. We find that several versions of a domestic-plus-border policy reduce emissions while increasing domestic production, whereas domestic or border policies alone support one policy objective at the expense of the other. Our results contribute to a growing body of literature on how climate and trade policies and outcomes may interact.

title: Will AI Grow Out of the Law's Control?

detail.abstract: Since September of 2026, a series of news stories exposed new risks that modern AI models might pose. AI agents deployed by OpenAI were found to have broken into a technology company's systems and several government websites. The Australian Prime Minister promised 'legal consequences', and a bill to ban superintelligence was introduced in the United States Congress. On the other hand, the Bank of England warned that the debts financing AI were becoming opaque and circular. These are usually treated as separate stories about safety, politics and finance. This commentary argues that they share a common premise. Indeed, the law tends to treat AI as being built (designed, finished and released), while its developers describe frontier AI as being "grown" and matured through training. Naturally, the conduct of a "grown" model is hard to foresee, and serious risks can arise before release, all while its financial market value is opaque. These features of AI tests different legal assumptions: (1) that harmful conduct can be traced to a human act; (2) that law should engage at release; and (3) that obligations are backed by assets of known value. The commentary explains each assumption and evaluates what current laws are capable of.

detail.abstract: The share of Latin America’s working-age population has begun to fall on the back of increased longevity and falling birth rates. The female participation response to falling child dependency is the largest domestic margin available to offset it. We quantify that margin, combining harmonized microdata from seven large economies with a tractable overlapping generations model in which female labor supply responds endogenously to household composition. We first decompose the region’s gender participation gap into several margins, with about one third arising from the differential labor supply response to household-composition between men and women (a ”motherhood penalty”). Embedding these estimates in a macro framework in which male and female labor can act as complements or substitutes, we find that the female participation response to falling child dependency can partially offset the demographic drag, raising regional GDP by between 3.1 and 11.3 percent by 2050 relative to a path with participation held fixed. The range reflects both fundamental uncertainty around future paths of comoving national trends and substantial heterogeneous labor supply responses across countries.

detail.abstract: The article examines governance models in transnational agri-food supply chains and the regulatory choices made at EU level to steer their development towards the sustainability paradigm. Building on a systemic reading of the supply chain as a legally relevant space, the analysis highlights the central role of contract as a tool for governing economic relations. At the same time, it exposes the limits of an approach that risks turning sustainability into a mere transfer of risks and compliance burdens onto agricultural producers, who remain structurally weaker actors within the value chain. From this standpoint, particular attention is devoted to Directive (EU) 2024/1760 on corporate sustainability due diligence, considered as a model for the institutionalisation of the chain of activities and for the accountability of lead firms through the contractual projection of sustainability obligations along the supply chain. The article argues, however, that the failure to treat price and purchasing practices as legally relevant variables weakens the effectiveness of the model, raising concerns that relate not only to the protection of the agricultural party, but also to the proper functioning of the internal market and to competition. The contribution concludes with a reflection on the structural tensions inherent in this emerging regulatory framework, suspended between the ambition to secure sustainable supply-chain governance and the recalibration introduced by Directive (EU) 2026/470.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of cropland extent reduction on child health outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and examines the moderating roles of household wealth and family size. Using geocoded data on over 336,000 children from Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and satellite-derived cropland extent data from GLAD (2000-2019), I employ two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimation with rainfall anomaly as an instrument for cropland reduction. Results show that cropland loss significantly reduces children's WAZ and WHZ scores and increases the likelihood of underweight and wasting, especially among the poorest households and larger families. The study contributes by using georeferenced point-level cropland extent as an objective spatial indicator of food availability, instrumented by exogenous rainfall anomaly. This offers new insights into the environmental determinants of child undernutrition in SSA.

detail.abstract: Long-term operation can make the offline calibration of a line-structured-light measurement system inconsistent with its current geometry. This paper presents a reference-assisted in-situ recalibration method for compensating bounded parameter drift around a high-precision offline calibration. A parameter-driven digital twin supplies paired stripe-centerline and parameter-residual samples for supervised initialization. A two-stage network first estimates camera intrinsics and distortion and then estimates the camera pose and laser-plane parameters after differentiable undistortion and normalization. During a scheduled idle traverse, the laser is projected onto a machine reference plane containing two markers with a pre-calibrated separation. Straightness, planarity, known-length, and temporal terms refine the bounded residual estimate in a 10-frame window. Six supplementary removal configurations were evaluated with five repeats, and the complete-method sequence was retained as the A7 reference. The complete method achieved a mean dynamic reprojection error of 0.374 px and reduced the error below 0.5 px after approximately nine input frames. On the reported 20-reading grinding-wheel sequence, the fixed offline system model produced outer- and inner-diameter absolute errors of 0.54 and 0.35 mm, whereas the reference-assisted update produced 0.02 mm for both. The calibration-stage computation required 50-80 ms per accepted frame, corresponding to a ceiling of approximately 12.5-20 Hz before acquisition, stripe extraction, and reconstruction. These results support local in-situ drift compensation within the calibrated operating envelope, but do not establish unrestricted scene generalization, high-frequency vibration tracking, or metrological traceability.

detail.abstract: There is a long-standing claim that government social spending crowds out private savings and charity. There is also a newer set of arguments claiming that access to private resources (home equity, credit, insurance, charity) dampens voters' support for public assistance and social insurance. These claims have not been jointly investigated nor has the literature connected workplace programs and benefits with either outcome. We investigate both sides of the "substitution hypothesis" in the context of an unstudied set of workplace private welfare programs: Employee Hardship Funds (EHFs). EHFs enable employers to distribute emergency cash to their workers using donations pooled from employees themselves. Using three original surveys, we find that state-level variation in the generosity of the social safety net is unrelated to worker support for or willingness to donate to EHFs. Experimental manipulation of EHF salience among workers at two large retailers indicates that EHFs do not displace support for public unemployment insurance or government emergency aid, regardless of the generosity of the EHF program. Workplace-based private welfare programs like EHFs appear unconnected with government social insurance programs in the minds of workers.

detail.abstract: The economy of Bangladesh has been on the rise over the past decade. One of the biggest factors contributing to the country's economic condition is the inflation rate. The increase in prices over a certain period is referred to as inflation. The project aimed to present a comprehensive analysis of forecasting the inflation rates in Bangladesh using Machine learning algorithms. The inflation rates are predicted using data over the last ten years. The data has been obtained from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics. This study predicts inflation rates based on the following factors: CPI Value, Currency against USD, Money Supply, Interest Rates, GDP (in BDT), and GDP Per Capita and compares the performance of numerous models, finding that XGBoost is the most efficient algorithm, with Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.193 and Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 0.062. Similarly, the Random forest model also performed better with low evaluation metrics. The findings indicate the exciting prospects of machine learning approaches for economic forecasting, particularly in emerging nations like Bangladesh.

detail.abstract: A state's ability to integrate energy, data and logistics flows into adaptive national capabilities determines its national competitiveness, resilience and influence. detail.abstract: A recorded terminal price can be close to a contract's payout while representing an old transaction rather than a contemporaneous market response. We examine this distinction in a fixed, bounded sample of twenty Kalshi markets drawn from a thirty-day lifecycle corpus. Two hundred metadata candidates were selected by hash rank without using prices or payout direction; 180 had both required lifecycle anchors, and twenty were frozen before price retrieval. Subsequent public API requests returned 10,801 distinct non-block trades and 4,067 one-minute candle records. Seventeen markets had transactions in the requested windows; three had none. Every returned trade preceded its market's recorded determination timestamp. Among the seventeen observed markets, the median age of the latest transaction timestamp was 400.71 seconds at determination and 614.78 seconds at settlement. Three markets had different transaction prices at their identical latest timestamps, requiring a set-valued rather than arbitrarily ordered terminal observation. Absolute distances from the subsequently recorded YES payout ranged from $0.001 to $0.12, with both bounds on the cross-market median equal to $0.01. Only 820 candle records combined positive volume with transaction OHLC; the remaining 3,247 contained either a previous-price value or no transaction-price object. We formalize the joint price-age observation and show why moving an unchanged observation to a later lifecycle anchor increases its age without demonstrating new price discovery. These are reproducible, descriptive results for a small terminal-recordconditioned sample, not estimates of causal market response, public contractual decidability, executable arbitrage, or venue-wide convergence.

detail.abstract: We study a sequential stochastic portfolio optimization problem in which the set of admissible assets depends on the data, predictive inputs are uncertain, risk-control parameters are state dependent, and execution decisions affect the state of the next optimization problem. We treat portfolio composition and total risky exposure as distinct decisions. We formalize the investable universe as an endogenous feasible-set operator and derive a score-margin stability condition. We then characterize an internally generated forward risk state produced by the scenario-based optimizer, derive conditions under which expected-return information distorts that signal, and construct a centered risk operator that removes this distortion. A horizon-diversified controller combines the resulting slow, model-implied risk state with fast realized volatility. Partial execution satisfies exact contraction and turnover identities, and the full policy is shown to be adapted to decision-time information. In our empirical study, the combined controller reduces maximum drawdown by more than 50% while delivering similar risk-adjusted performance across 83 monthly walk-forward decisions on 220 U.S. exchange-traded funds. Mechanism tests isolate timing effects from mechanical exposure reduction and transaction-cost effects.

detail.abstract: Standard theories trace information asymmetry to privately held information, heterogeneous signals, or costly information acquisition. We identify a distinct mechanism: otherwise identical rational agents observing a common Markov state at asynchronous times can form different predictive distributions because their information differs in age, thereby generating asymmetric information. When the transition kernel separates information ages, independent Bernoulli observation arrivals make such divergence recur infinitely often almost surely, even with identical arrival probabilities. When agents instead choose costly updating intensities, independent update realizations can regenerate heterogeneous information ages among ex ante identical agents. In a stationary Gaussian AR(1) environment, the consequences depend on common staleness as well as the age gap: holding the gap fixed, older information raises individual uncertainty while reducing expected squared forecast disagreement and the value of certifying relative freshness. This generates stale consensus: low disagreement despite high uncertainty. With multiple ordered ages, costly certification supports partial-unraveling equilibria in which fresher types certify and sufficiently stale types pool. Under geometric information ages, more frequent updating weakly lowers the smallest and largest equilibrium disclosure cutoffs wherever positive-certification equilibria exist. The framework has implications for credit, insurance, financial markets, and multi-agent AI.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms' use of targeted advertising harms both consumers and markets. Industry giants, able to collect vast amounts of quality data, allows them to create personalized ads that tempt users into purchases based on past preferences and predicted needs. As most users are unaware that their data enables platforms to manipulate their shopping habits, these advertisements become a source of information asymmetry, keeping consumers from seeking out other options. This results in variated prices, decreased innovation, and-ultimately-a lessening of competition. Without sufficient consumer knowledge, the market cannot correct itself, and the government must step in. An examination of various laws in Taiwan indicates that labeling targeted advertising an "obviously unfair practice" would enable competition authorities to identify legitimate competitive harms and enact flexible solutions that help maintain free and fair competition in digital marketplaces. Such a model will allow other jurisdictions to develop proactive competition law policies that are able to address the quick changes that occur in the rapidly developing digital economy.

detail.abstract: The study of long-run technological change depends on access to full patent texts, yet none exist for United States patents prior to 1976. Researchers have instead relied on bibliometric proxies such as citation counts and technology class assignments, which capture little of the technical substance recorded in patent specifications. We present CLEARPAT, a dataset of high-fidelity full texts for 3.9 million U.S. utility patents granted between 1836 and 1975, alongside title, date, and patentee records for 9,462 patents granted from 1790. Full texts are produced by a dual-OCR pipeline in which two vision-language engines process digitized patent images and a large language model adjudicates conflicts between their outputs, substantially reducing character error rates relative to single-engine OCR. We extract and validate all key fields, including claims, descriptions, inventor details, geocoded locations, and citations. CLEARPAT appends to born-digital USPTO records from 1976 onward, yielding a continuous record of American patenting from 1790 to the present, with full text from 1836, and supporting research on technological change, knowledge diffusion, and science-technology relationships.

detail.abstract: The same price move and trading volume can reflect very different changes in who is investing, what investors believe, and which positions they are able to take. This paper develops a market-clearing framework for interpreting such price-volume patterns by relating price changes to the reallocation of positions across investors and by combining these outcomes with additional market data. Reallocation is the more informative measure of investor adjustment because trading volume can include repeated and intermediary trading. The central concept is market tension, the pressure created when, before the market adjusts, the positions investors want under new conditions differ from the positions they already hold. Market clearing resolves this pressure through some combination of price adjustment and position reallocation. When free float is unchanged, reallocation lies between the total buying and selling pressure contained in market tension, so price and reallocation restrict the underlying transition but generally do not pin it down. How strongly prices move depends on the market's local absorption capacity. Understanding where that capacity comes from requires separating price responsiveness from participation and actual holdings. The framework therefore distinguishes three market concepts for each stock: its specific market, the investors for whom the stock is investable; its realized market, the investors who actually carry a position; and its responsive market, the investors whose reactions to price provide local absorption capacity. Because these markets can diverge, holdings alone do not establish who participates or how much the market can absorb, while an isolated investor entry or exit that moves the price can reveal that capacity. Shortsale constraints determine which pessimistic views reach the market: other things equal, tighter constraints raise equilibrium prices or leave them unchanged, while changes in shorting costs or access provide additional information through prices and position reallocation. Closing-auction, holdings, participation, free-float, and securities-lending data can help distinguish transitions that look alike in price and volume.

detail.abstract: Customer segmentation tells a card issuer which customers are likely to run into trouble. It does not tell the issuer what to do about it. In this paper I take the behavioral segments from my earlier work and use them to build the decision that segmentation leaves out: given what I know about a customer's vulnerability and the current state of the economy, should I act now, and if so how, or should I wait? I write this as a Markov decision process. The state pairs a behavioral vulnerability tier with a macroeconomic scenario, the actions are the levers an issuer actually has (changing the credit limit, repricing, offering a retention incentive, or converting a balance to installments), and the objective is risk-adjusted portfolio profit over a two-year horizon. The idea that drives the model is to put each customer's recovery probability, meaning the chance that a stressed account fixes itself without any help, directly into the reward, so that a customer who would recover on their own is not treated the same as one heading for a permanent loss. The model also lets customers walk away: harsher actions raise the chance a customer voluntarily closes the account, which builds behavioral feedback into the decision. I calibrate the model to public delinquency behavior and to the four-segment structure of my 2025 study and solve it by backward induction. The dynamically optimized policy raises risk-adjusted portfolio value by about 27 percent over a static "maintain" rule and lowers the two-year charge-off rate from 19.9 percent to 12.0 percent, at the cost of somewhat higher voluntary attrition (23.3 percent against 19.4 percent), which is the behavioral price of intervening. I run the policy along two very different historical stress paths, the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis and the 1979 to 1982 Volcker disinflation, and it preserves 38 to 43 percent more value while cutting charge-offs by roughly 37 to 38 percent against the static rule. I also formalize the CARD Act restriction on retroactive repricing as a hard constraint, and find that it costs about 2.1 percent of value when customers cannot leave but becomes slack once attrition is modeled, because the risk of losing customers already deters the repricing the rule targets. A separately trained Q-learning agent recovers the same policy in 90 percent of states, and the policy holds under a plus or minus 20 percent shift in the default-hazard calibration (95 percent of states unchanged). As a first step toward grounding the model in data, I re-estimate the tier structure and baseline hazards from the UCI "Default of Credit Card Clients" panel of 30,000 accounts: the four-tier vulnerability structure reappears cleanly in the data, and the optimal policy is unchanged in 95 percent of states, though the value of acting dynamically moderates from about 27 percent to about 9 percent once the empirically closer risk tiers are used. This is a calibrated, normative model rather than an empirical estimation, and every input is built to be replaced with an issuer's own numbers.

detail.abstract: These notes, prepared for the NYSBA Labor and Employment Law Section Fall Meeting, offer a broad look at wages and New York State law. The U.S. relies more than its Western peers on wages to allocate basic goods like healthcare, housing, and retirement, and the rapid rise of large language models threatens the centrality of human labor that arrangement depends on. Most New Yorkers, though, face more immediate problems: blurry classification lines and fissured workplaces, broad statutory exclusions, low union coverage, arbitration, weak federal enforcement, and immigration pressure at the bottom of the labor market. I sketch what states can do: widen coverage, open routes into protection for non-employees, extend union reach, and enforce aggressively against wage theft. New York has already moved on several of these fronts, and there is still low-hanging fruit to pick.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a local information-geometric theory for statistical representations and structural boundaries. The central objective is not to enumerate yet another collection of mutually isolated identifiability conditions, but to establish a mathematical chain that can be audited layer by layer: how structural differences generate statistical differences, how relative entropy near a boundary determines the natural local scale, and when parameter-independent representation compression changes that scale. We first write the composite representation from structure to invariant measure to observation to statistic as T = S ∘ K ∘ ν, and, under quantitative separation moduli and local Fréchet structure, derive layerwise criteria for blind spots. We then introduce a controlled random probe: an external, parameter-independent, and controllable random perturbation ρE is injected before a nonlinear statistical functional, with V_ρ(P) = E_{X∼P,E}[ψ(X + ρE)]. Under finite smoothness and moment conditions, we prove an explicit finite-order expansion of the probe difference. Its first nonzero derivative–moment coefficient exactly determines the order at which the probe becomes visible. This yields a deterministic criterion for “lifting” a blind spot to a higher order and provides a fully analytic exact example showing that a statistic that is strictly invisible at ρ = 0 can acquire a second-order visible signal under a controlled random probe. This result is distinct from ex post noise addition: the probe acts before the nonlinear statistic and therefore changes the observation experiment itself, rather than attempting to recover information already lost.

For a two-regime threshold model, we further generalize local boundary information from a scalar density to a boundary relative-entropy information measure defined on the threshold axis. Under general heterogeneous design, we define the matrix-valued measure B_∂(A) = E[ZZ^⊤ 1{S ∈ A}], and prove that the candidate-threshold relative entropy in the Gaussian threshold experiment is exactly the boundary information measure over the misclassification interval. When G has a density g, the measure has the explicit density ι_∂(s) = g(s)/(2σ²) Δθ^⊤ M(s) Δθ. At the same time, under general heterogeneous design we obtain an exact matrix representation of the population least-squares loss, L(τ) − L(τ*) = Δθ^⊤ Ω_±(τ) Δθ, where Ω_± is the matrix parallel sum of the misclassification information matrix and the background information matrix. We prove 0 ⪯ Ω_± ⪯ B_± and, under local nondegeneracy, obtain first-order equivalence between population loss and KL divergence without requiring completely homogeneous design.

To unify regular and nonregular local scales, we define the local relative-entropy order β: if KL(P_h ‖ P_0) = c|h|^β + o(|h|^β), then the relative-entropy budget of n independent observations reaches constant order at h_n ≍ n^{−1/β}. If the output representation is generated by a parameter-independent Markov channel, the data processing inequality implies that the output local relative-entropy order cannot be smaller than the input order. If a strict order jump β_U > β_X occurs, then on the natural local scale of the input experiment the output experiment has vanishing total variation, yielding a strict sense of “resolution degradation.” When the orders coincide, one can define the asymptotic relative-entropy fidelity coefficient η = c_U/c_X ∈ [0,1]. This chain places identifiability, information fidelity, and local resolution on a common local experimental scale.

Finally, we define the statistical visibility order α and establish a finite-order Fréchet transfer theorem together with a local Hölder composition law, explicitly distinguishing the visibility order α from the relative-entropy order β. The Hopf normal form is used only as an analytic validation example, showing that different statistical functionals can generate different visibility orders; no claim is made of being the first to discover Hopf observable singularity. Fisher information, Gaussian common-design calibration, three-regime global masking, and sample consistency are included as calibration, counterexample, and interface results. The paper is purely theoretical: it uses no empirical data, numerical simulations, parameter fitting, or plots. The principal results are derived analytically from probability measures, matrix projections, and statistical-experiment theory.

detail.abstract: This paper examines tariffs, their classification, and their role in international trade, with a particular focus on tariffs imposed by the United States on imported goods in 2025. It explores the main reasons behind the use of tariffs, including protecting domestic industries, supporting local production, addressing trade imbalances, and influencing international trade relations. The paper also examines the economic consequences of these policies for the United States and other countries. While tariffs can provide protection to certain domestic industries, they can also increase the cost of imported goods, leading businesses to raise prices and, ultimately, affecting consumers. These effects can extend beyond the United States through changes in global supply chains, production costs, and international trade. The paper argues that although tariffs can serve as a useful tool for achieving economic and strategic objectives, they may also create broader economic pressures by increasing prices, disrupting trade, and encouraging retaliatory measures from trading partners. Overall, this study highlights how U.S. tariff policies can have consequences that reach beyond national borders and influence businesses, consumers, and markets across the global economy.

detail.abstract: This paper tackles the long-standing debate over kurtosis measures-specifically whether they're defined by peakedness or the tails-by introducing the novel idea that kurtosis is a scale-free measure of dispersion. We establish this paradigm axiomatically, utilizing the concept of stochastic ordering between random variables normalized by an L p norm. By comparing the inversion of Pearson's kurtosis and the re-introduction of Geary's kurtosis, we develop two generalized, parameterized measures of kurtosis. We also define the rumps of a distribution and create a new non-kurtosis measure for 'tail-fatness'. After comparing kurtosis with established scale-free measures of dispersion, we compare kurtosis measures for a diverse array of distributions. Finally, we apply these constructs to the daily log-returns of the NYSE Index over four separate decades, revealing a consistency of kurtosis over time that challenges conventional assumptions.

detail.abstract: We use density forecasts from the U.S. Survey of Professional Forecasters to decompose aggregate forecast uncertainty into disagreement and average individual uncertainty. Disagreement accounts for only about 20% of aggregate uncertainty on average, but its contribution rises to about one half during recessions. Both components are countercyclical and positively related to GDP growth volatility, while disagreement measured from density forecasts displays stronger cyclical dynamics than conventional point-forecast disagreement. We rationalize these findings with a twosector heterogeneous-beliefs model in which forecasters learn about a latent growth component and differ in their perceived volatility.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified local interface from finite-dimensional Itô stochastic dynamical systems to statistical representation spaces and, building on earlier two-scale results, formulates a more complete local visibility structure. Its basic architecture has four mutually linked layers: the first nonzero jet order r along a parameter direction, the corresponding activation exponent γ of the leading coefficient as the dynamical noise scale σ ↓ 0, a nested filtration of invisible directions, and successive obstruction maps generated by recursive lifting of partial parameter jets. This yields an auditable framework linking stochastic dynamics, statistical representation, and local information geometry, without treating any single Fisher correction or Kramers formula as a universal noise law. First, under a common dominating measure and quadratic-integrability regularity, we prove the conditional-score orthogonal projection decomposition between quenched and annealed Fisher information, I q F = I a F + E[Cov(sq | Y )]  I a F , and derive the associated KL chain-rule information budget and data-processing contraction under parameter-independent Markov compression. Second, for a stable linear stochastic system with a stationary Gaussian snapshot experiment, we establish an exact Fisher formula, noise monotonicity, and a Fisher–KL–signal identity as a computable benchmark, without extending this benchmark to general stochastic systems. Third, we define the local random visibility signature χT (µ∗, v) = (r, γ), prove its invariance under regular parameterization and regular noise-scale transformations, and establish the transfer law (r, γ) 7→ (kr, kγ) under critical statistical representation composition. Fourth, we define a nested hierarchy of directional invisible sets Z σ k and then consider higher-order jets of parameter curves; the problem of removing kth-order visibility can be recursively reduced to a lifting equation in a linear image space, yielding a successive obstruction tower. In particular, the second-order obstruction is represented by the quotient-space class [D2Tσ(µ∗)[v, v]]; when it is nonzero, no local parameter curve with first-order tangent v can lift statistical invisibility to second order. More generally, the kth-order obstruction is defined on the space of liftable (k−1)st-order partial jets, rather than being incorrectly represented as a single invariant depending only on the initial direction. Fifth, under an additional two-parameter polyhomogeneous expansion, we introduce the visibility bigraded spectrum Specvis and its associated graded layers, and prove that the joint scaling t = σ βu projects the bidegree (r, γ) to the single exponent γ + βr. Furthermore, within a finite-dimensional real-analytic statisticalrepresentation subclass, we construct a Koszul filtered complex constrained by representation components and derive a genuine spectral sequence from the m-adic filtration; its first nontrivial differential reads the linearly visible layer, while later differentials organize higher-order jet constraints on local statistical fibers. Sixth, we establish a Fisher–KL two-scale bridge for general regular statistical readouts: if Dσ,v(t) ∼ Cσγ |t| r , then 2 KL ∼ JQC 2σ 2γ |t| 2r , and repeated observations induce the information-scale resolution law |t|res  N −1/(2r)σ −γ/r . When r > 1, first-order Fisher information can be exactly degenerate while KL remains positively separated at higher order, so Fisher corresponds precisely to the first-order sector of the local visibility structure. Finally, through regular-parameterized stochastic potential families, critical statistical readouts, finite-observation-window Eyring–Kramers scales, and a zero-noise invariantmeasure cluster theorem, we demonstrate the constructibility of the framework, its dynamical interface, and its scope limits. The central theoretical contribution is an independently auditable organizing principle: local structural response in random statistical representation is encoded by the chain two-scale signature – invisible filtration – successive obstruction – bigraded associated layer, with a strict filtered-complex spectral-sequence realization in a finite-dimensional analytic subclass, and Fisher and KL serving as statistical transfer mechanisms.

detail.abstract: This chapter analyses how the Digital Omnibus on AI recalibrates the AI Act’s framework regarding AI regulatory sandboxes, focusing on the amendments to Articles 57, 58, and 60. The Digital Omnibus on AI preserves the basic architecture of the sandboxes but adapts and refocuses it, postponing the requirement for Member States to establish at least one national sandbox to August 2027 (compared to the original deadline of August 2026) and realigning it with the postponement of other implementation deadlines, particularly for the requirements concerning high-risk systems. At the same time, it introduces the possibility of establishing an EU-wide sandbox, managed by the AI Office, for systems falling under Article 75(1)—that is, systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider—thereby strengthening a multilevel experimental governance framework. Further amendments clarify the content of the governance rules to be included in the European Commission’s implementing acts and the relationship between sandboxes and real-world testing, laying the groundwork for closer integration between experimentation and the implementation of the AI Act.

title: Are Factors Always Paid Their Marginal Products? Input Bundles and the Labour Share in Indian Organised Manufacturing

detail.abstract:
Since Clark in the late nineteenth century, marginal-productivity theory has read factor shares as output elasticities, and labour-share analysis has treated all non-labour income as capital income. But are factors always paid their marginal products? This paper develops a common framework for factor-share analysis that accommodates technological contributions, remuneration gaps and externally estimated output-market markups. It shows that under an increasing, binding employment-capacity constraint with a positive shadow value, which ties labour and capital into an input bundle, a price-taking producer can pay labour below its marginal product and capital above its own at a global profit maximum, without the employer power to which Robinson traced such gaps; the common multiplier links the two remuneration gaps. The labour share is then the labour elasticity times remuneration incidence (pay relative to marginal product), and non-labour income splits into capital's elasticity, the capital-side share of the labour gap and residual income. Estimated as a translog system, the framework nests the conventional decomposition as a special case. In Indian organised manufacturing, the labour share fell by 10.72 points between 2001-02 and 2006-07 and rose from 19.8 to 31.7 per cent between 2007-08 and 2023-24. Remuneration incidence accounts for most of both movements, 9.98 of the fall and 6.91 of the rise, against 1.52 for the labour elasticity; the rise came out of residual income, not capital payments. The medium-establishment result survives omitting the capital-payment equation; the large-establishment and combined rankings depend on retaining it. The findings point to relaxing the equality of factor payments and marginal products as a maintained assumption in factor pricing: labour-share accounts should report remuneration incidence and the split of non-labour income alongside the share, since a rising share may reflect how pay moves relative to fitted marginal products, not technology alone.

title: Complete Identifiability and Cross-Model Rigidity of Relative-Norm Observations: Conformal Quotients, Gauge Selection, Markov Flexibility, and the Fisher–Finsler Boundary
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Complete Identifiability and Cross-Model Rigidity of Relative-Norm Observations: Conformal Quotients, Gauge Selection, Markov Flexibility, and the Fisher–Finsler Boundary

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
This paper treats the relative-norm observation S_{F,ξ}(v) = F(v)/F(ξ) as a genuine observation map, rather than interpreting it in advance as a normalization formula for some known metric. The central questions are: what exactly does this observation identify, what are all of its unidentifiable degrees of freedom, and under what conditions can statistical naturality eliminate some or all of these freedoms? We establish a rigorous chain from observational identifiability to statistical rigidity.

First, for general smooth absolutely positively one-homogeneous fiber norms, we prove a complete observation-quotient theorem: two norms produce the same relative observation if and only if they differ by a unique positive smooth pointwise factor; hence the observation space is in bijection, in the set-theoretic sense, with the quotient by positive conformal rescalings. This conclusion uses neither the parallelogram law nor any Fisher structure. Second, under the parallelogram law, the Jordan–von Neumann polarization theorem shows that every admissible observation uniquely determines a smooth Riemannian metric normalized along the reference direction, and we give an exact description of the scale coordinate and of all set-theoretic sections. Third, on the finite probability simplex, we prove a symmetry no-go theorem for intrinsic selection of the reference direction: there is no everywhere-nonzero tangent reference field that is natural under all permutations, showing that the reference-direction gauge cannot be selected intrinsically from global symmetry alone. Fourth, on the fixed binary simplex, we completely classify all positive one-dimensional Riemannian metrics that are monotone under all interior-preserving binary Markov affine maps, obtaining w(1−p) = w(p) and p²w(p) nondecreasing, and equivalently derive a differential inequality for the Fisher conformal factor. This yields an infinite-dimensional flexibility cone and an explicit non-Fisher continuous family, rather than reducing the non-uniqueness of the binary single-model case to a single counterexample. Fifth, within the Fisher conformal orbit, we establish a general propagation mechanism for the conformal factor along Fisher-isometric embeddings admitting Markov left inverses, and prove that a strictly reduced Markov family generated by one fixed binary anchor already forces all pointwise conformal factors to collapse to the same global constant. Sixth, we extend the Markov contraction construction on the Finsler side from the single L⁴ example to the even-integer L^{2k} family and sharpen the dimensional threshold for non-Hilbert counterexamples to n = 3; when n = 2, no non-Hilbert norm exists because the tangent space is one-dimensional. Finally, we place the existing Fisher-uniqueness results of Čencov, Nagaoka, Ay–Jost–Lê–Schwachhöfer, and Lê at explicitly declared external interfaces, rather than presenting external uniqueness statements as internal proofs of this paper. The resulting structure is the unified chain “observation quotient—gauge selection—single-model flexibility—cross-model rigidity—Fisher representative—Finsler boundary.”

detail.abstract: Sri Lanka crossed a demographic threshold most countries reach only after they have grown rich, it is ageing fast while its public finances are still recovering from a sovereign default. This paper revisits a 2015 assessment of that collision and updates it against the country's 2024 census, its ongoing IMF program, and the pension reform debate now underway in Colombo. Two trends have moved in opposite directions since 2015. Population ageing has accelerated, the over 65 shares of the population reached 12.6 percent at the 2024 census, and overall dependency climbed to 49.8 percent. Meanwhile the public finances available to absorb that cost have shrunk, not grown, revenue collapsed after 2022 and is only now being rebuilt under IMF monitored reform. The paper examines three fiscal channels through which ageing presses onto the budget, health expenditure, the public service pension system, and the shrinking base of working age taxpayers funding both. It finds that Sri Lanka's pension system, in particular, is not just expensive but regressive (nearly half of public service pension payments go to the richest fifth of pensioners), and that the contributory pension fund now being proposed is a necessary but politically difficult fix. The paper closes by arguing that ageing and fiscal consolidation cannot be treated as separate problems in Sri Lanka's recovery, the design of one determines whether the other is sustainable.

title: A Multi-Relation Attention Method for Oil Production Forecasting in Injection-Production Well Networks​
affiliations: Southwest Petroleum University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Southwest Petroleum University and Southwest Petroleum University

detail.abstract: Reliable short-term oil-production forecasting in waterflooded injection-production well networks requires both the target well’s temporal evolution and heterogeneous cross-well dependencies. This study formulates a 7-d multistep forecasting task and proposes the Multi-site Prediction Method based on Multi-relation Attention (MPM-MRA). A gated recurrent unit learns the target well’s self-history trend, while three relation-specific branches represent dynamic production synergy, shared injection-response similarity, and static proxy attributes. Relation-level attention and temporal encoding combine these branches as a controlled correction to the self-history forecast. The shared injection-response relation captures statistical similarity between production wells responding to common injection signals and is used as a predictive proxy for coordinated behavior rather than a direct representation of subsurface fluid connectivity. Experiments used daily records from 58 production wells and 55 injection wells in a Chinese waterflooded field, with 30 d of observations used to forecast the next 7 d. Across repeated runs, MPM-MRA achieved an RMSE of 0.3616±0.0156 m³/d, an MAE of 0.1476±0.0098 m³/d, and R² of 0.7941±0.0182, giving the best mean error profile among the compared learning-based models. Paired tests supported selected error differences; given the small repeat sample, these tests are interpreted as supplementary run-level robustness evidence. Ablation results identified the static proxy and shared injection-response branches as the principal sources of structural correction, and auxiliary well-group analysis showed locally concentrated relation patterns. The proposed decomposition provides relation-aware short-term forecasts and structured information for production monitoring, key-well screening, and review of wells during injection-production adjustments.

detail.abstract: We examine whether democracy affects the quality of official statistics by focusing on historically colonized countries. To address endogeneity concerns, we use historical settler mortality as an instrument, following the logic that settler mortality shaped colonial settlement strategies and long-run institutional development, including democratic institutions. This approach estimates the democracy-statistical quality relationship among the complier group-colonies whose democratic trajectories were influenced by settler mortality-while recognizing that settler mortality may also capture broader colonial institutional legacies. This complier group is policyrelevant because many post-colonial states continue to face state-capacity and data quality challenges, making it especially important to understand whether democratic institutions may help improve official statistics. Using cross-sectional data from 2023, combining the Economist Intelligence Unit's Democracy Index and the World Bank's Statistical Performance Indicators overall index, we estimate that a one-unit increase in democracy is associated with a 5.3-6.2-point increase in the quality of official statistics. We further find suggestive evidence that this estimated relationship is heterogeneous: it is about 3.7 points larger in common-law countries and 3.6 points smaller in civil-law countries, suggesting that colonial legal traditions may make democracy's relationship with statistical quality stronger in some countries and weaker in others.
