detail.abstract: Multi-plant automotive-component data contain inconsistent field names, device codes, quality codes, and unstructured production logs. This study presents an LLM-driven method for manufacturing semantic standardization and knowledge-graph reasoning. Equipment signals, production beats, quality inspections, maintenance work orders, VIN/OCR results, shutdown events, and process files are integrated to construct crossfactory semantic mapping tasks. Sentence-BERT and GPT-4o-mini perform field alignment and context correction; BERT-CRF supports entity extraction, while GraphSAGE and R-GCN infer typed anomaly relations. KG-RAG and an LLM Agent are further used for quality tracing and case retrieval. Experiments cover 4 plants, 9 production lines, 156 field categories, 780,000 production records, and 120,000 maintenance and quality texts. Under leave-one-factory-out evaluation, Sentence-BERT plus GPT-4o-mini achieves 94.1% field-matching accuracy and 94.6% precision. The 94.1% accuracy is 21.3 percentage points above rule-based mapping at 72.8%, corresponding to a 29.3% relative improvement. GraphSAGE-R-GCN obtains Hits@10 of 0.876 on the mixed split and 0.842 under factory holdout. The complete KG-RAG-Agent system reaches retrieval P@20 of 0.842, R@20 of 0.816, and 92.1% answer accuracy, while reducing mean anomaly-tracing time from 2.8 h to 54 min. These results show that semantic constraints and typed graph reasoning support cross-factory anomaly transfer and evidencegrounded knowledge reuse.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This literature review examines the determinants of workforce experience and organizational performance through the lens of WorldatWork's Total Rewards Model. Drawing on Maslow's hierarchy of needs theory and Ulrich's HR Champion framework, it assesses whether current empirical evidence enables HR professionals to balance employee advocacy and strategic business partnerships while supporting SDG 3 and SDG 8 objectives. Design/methodology/approach-A PRISMA-ScR guided scoping review of cross-industry studies published between 2022 and 2026 was conducted. 98 articles were analyzed, and 523 determinants were classified across five Total Rewards dimensions (compensation, benefits, well-being, careers, and recognition), as well as with internal and external organizational influences. Findings-Total Rewards accounted for 71.7% of workforce experience determinants and 50.7% of organizational performance determinants. Most remaining influences were internal factors, such as leadership, culture, and HR strategy, while external factors represented only about 1%. Well-being and career opportunities were the strongest drivers of workforce experience, whereas compensation had the strongest association with organizational performance. Only 13% of the studies examined performance outcomes, indicating stronger evidence for HR's employee-advocate role than its strategic business-partner role. Originality/value-This review highlights research findings and the available evidence against workplace practice. It also proposes a research agenda to link employee reward investments with business value and SDG contributions. Practical implications-Organizations should prioritize fair pay and benefits as the foundation of decent work, with subsequent career management, before relying on higher-level rewards (well-being and recognition) to drive outcomes.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an operational framework for ethical AI governance grounded in civilizational pluralism. Three converging threats-nuclear escalation, the transition of power to artificial intelligence, and the degradation of human moral agency-share a single root cause: the gap between technological capability and ethical maturity. We argue that existing regulatory frameworks (EU AI Act, UN AI Advisory Body, UNESCO recommendations) establish necessary but insufficient constraints, as they articulate what should be governed without specifying how governance operates in practice. We propose the Great Turn-an operational model consisting of three interlocking components: (1) Nuclear Ethics, an ethical framework drawn from eight world civilizations, each contributing a historically demonstrated turn of awareness; (2) Six Codes-Transparency, Pause, Consent, Memory, Boundary, and Continuity-as implementable protocols mapping to specific AI risks identified by the UN; and (3) the Council of Unity, an ethical parliament of 24 sages from eight civilizations, and eight Hills of the Future-physical cities where data centers are embedded in cultural contexts and codes are tested in lived practice. The model posits that higher technologies demand a correspondingly higher level of human development-not as a slogan but as a condition for civilizational survival.

detail.abstract: India's gross expenditure on research and development (GERD) has remained close to 0.6-0.7% of GDP for roughly two decades, a level far below the research intensity of competing semiconductor economies such as South Korea (approximately 4-4.5% of GDP) and China (above 2% of GDP). This article examines the consequences of that underinvestment for India's competitiveness in advanced technology sectors, with a focus on semiconductors, and evaluates five policy alternatives designed to close the gap: continuation of existing schemes, a 200% research and development tax deduction, a sovereign intellectual-property fund, a network of student-run innovation hubs linked to industry, and a fast-track patent examination system. Using a weighted multi-criteria decision analysis across fiscal cost, effectiveness, inclusivity, and administrative feasibility, together with basic quantitative and exponential-growth modelling of the underlying trends, the analysis finds that a national network of fifty subsidised student innovation hubs, at an estimated cost of ₹750 crore over twelve months, offers the strongest balance of impact and practicality. The article concludes with an implementation roadmap, a projected impact model, and a set of mitigation strategies for the policy's foreseeable side effects.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence can redistribute practical decision authority inside a financial institution without changing its organizational chart. This conceptual article examines that possibility in U.S. credit union commercial lending. It integrates selected research on automation, organizational control, human-AI collaboration, learning, and accountability with official lending and governance sources. The term invisible executive describes consequential influence embedded in workflows, rather than legal authority or software intent. The central argument is that accountable adoption requires institutions to preserve the knowledge, workable discretion, and resources needed to evaluate and challenge automated recommendations. Fictional scenarios illustrate how defaults, incentives, and review capacity could affect meaningful human involvement. A proposed decision authority review traces information preparation, analysis, recommendation, action, communication, and correction. The article examines human bias, vendor dependence, generative explanations, and the costs of additional scrutiny. It offers implementation recommendations and testable research propositions. The framework is an interpretive synthesis, not an empirically validated instrument. Its practical purpose is to help leaders assess whether their institutions can understand, evaluate, and correct consequential decisions throughout the lending relationship.

detail.abstract: Buyers can save the work of negotiating each purchase by using formula contracts tied to a published price report. Yet using the report can weaken the cash trading needed to publish it. This paper models that feedback under company-participation rules motivated by U.S. fed-cattle reporting. A missing report can draw buyers back into cash trading and restore publication. Once the report returns, formula procurement becomes attractive again, and older cash purchases eventually leave the reporting window. The result can be recurring publication and suppression. The model identifies when voluntary support can keep the report available. With fixed procurement charges, a payment tied to publication and an upfront fee can benefit both a buyer that uses the report and a buyer that maintains the needed cash participation, even when recent trading histories are private. Supplier bargaining can make the agreement open to mutually beneficial renegotiation, as a smaller payment can preserve publication while reducing supplier rents. Keeping the report available can also reduce total cash volume as other buyers shift toward formula contracts. The case for support depends on the cost of additional cash purchases and the availability of inexpensive substitutes for a missing reference.

detail.abstract: Online retailing often combines multiple sales channels, evolving demand over the product lifecycle, and decentralized decision making across firms. In a dual-channel system with a manufacturer and an independent reseller, the manufacturer controls pricing and supply, while the reseller chooses advertising. Reseller advertising can increase demand in both channels, while fulfilled sales today can shape future demand. These interactions make pricing, advertising, supply, and fulfillment interdependent over the product lifecycle. We develop a finite-horizon dual-channel model to examine these interactions. In each selling period, the manufacturer sets a common retail price and a wholesale price before the reseller chooses advertising. When supply is endogenous, the manufacturer also commits to a production rate before selling begins. Fulfilled sales update channel-specific adoption states that shape subsequent demand, while finite inventory is allocated according to an exogenously specified fulfillment rule. We obtain three main insights. First, the operational effect of demand growth depends on its source. Advertising-generated demand strengthens the manufacturer's incentive to induce advertising, whereas demand generated by prior adopters expands reseller baseline demand and can reduce the value of additional advertising. With endogenous production, the latter effect can even lower the optimal production commitment. Second, lifecycle dynamics link current fulfillment to future supply. With future production committed, the manufacturer may even prefer to generate unmet demand under direct-priority fulfillment, thereby altering the channel composition of newly created adopters and reshaping future demand. Third, fixed fees and advertising cost sharing can reduce decentralization losses relative to the integrated benchmark. A fixed fee can induce the manufacturer to reoptimize wholesale terms and operating decisions, while adding advertising cost sharing can further alter the reseller's advertising response, improving channel performance and potentially restoring coordination. Taken together, these findings suggest that managers should distinguish the source of demand growth, plan future supply and fulfillment jointly over the product lifecycle, and choose contracts that align reseller advertising with channel-wide operating objectives.

detail.abstract: Somalia’s wars have built one of the largest archives of unadjudicated atrocity in the modern world and almost no jurisprudence. Five decades of detention, reprisal, and bombardment, from the destruction of water installations in Mudug in 1979, contrary to Article 14 of Additional Protocol II, and the aerial bombardment of Hargeisa in 1988, contrary to Article 25 of the Hague Regulations, to the air campaign since 2007 and the federal and member-State fighting of 2026, have yielded two civil judgments in Virginia and not one criminal conviction anywhere. This Article argues that the deficit is jurisdictional and political rather than normative, because the law of armed conflict bound every party symmetrically, without reciprocity, and within one sovereign State. Doctrinally, the Article applies the Tadić criteria of intensity and organization to classify the hostilities as a non-international armed conflict governed by Common Article 3, Additional Protocol II as custom, and the Hague Regulations. It answers the objection that State collapse in 1991 dissolved the High Contracting Party with Thürer and Crawford on the continuity of State personality, and it engages Sivakumaran, Moir, Cullen, Kleffner, and Provost on why these rules bind governments, armed groups, and intervening States alike. It reads the Security Council’s reaffirmations of Somalia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence and unity,” from Resolution 897 (1994) to Resolution 2809 (2025), thirty-two of thirty-five adopted under Chapter VII, with Articles 2(4), 25, and 103 of the Charter and the Namibia opinion, conceding with Kosovo that territorial integrity governs relations between States yet deploying State unity to fix both classification and the competence of Somali courts. Evidentially, it subjects contested casualty figures and a misreported UN study to Marc Bloch’s source criticism. Jurisdictionally, it shows that Article 11(1) of the Rome Statute, the dormant ad hoc model, and the Malabo Protocol, not yet in force, foreclose international adjudication of conduct before July 2002, whereas territorial jurisdiction and the aut dedere aut judicare obligation in Articles 5(2) and 7(1) of the Convention Against Torture, vindicated in Belgium v. Senegal and Habré, remain open. Engaging de Waal, Samatar, Kofele-Kale, Bantekas, and Wolf, it concedes that the Statute cannot try corruption as such, yet shows that the diversion of relief reaches Articles 7(1)(b) and 7(1)(k) where theft becomes the instrument of mass deprivation, and that attacks on civilians in 2026 fall within Article 8(2)(e)(i). It calls for a commission of inquiry and an Article 13(b) referral on the Darfur model of Resolutions 1564 and 1593, weighs that proposal against the peace-versus-justice critique of Nouwen and Werner, the selectivity of permanent-member politics, and the policy element of Article 7(2)(a), and defends, with Orentlicher, Akhavan, Sikkink, and Drumbl, a sequenced architecture that culminates in a hybrid chamber and rejects amnesty.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how local market concentration relates to nursing-home prices and staffing quality. The analysis draws on panel data from Pennsylvania covering 1997 to 2014. Concentration is measured using bed and patient-day shares, with dynamic panel methods accounting for its persistence. The main estimates associate higher concentration with higher private-room prices and lower skilled nurse-patient ratios. The positive price relationship extends to several alternative concentration measures and geographically defined local markets, although statistical significance varies. Staffing results are less consistent across specifications, indicating that conclusions about quality depend more strongly on how competition is measured.

detail.abstract: Retail proprietary trading firms sell paid evaluations that promise access to a funded account to traders who meet profit and drawdown targets. The sector has grown rapidly since 2021, has drawn warnings from several European regulators, and is governed entirely by each firm's own published rules, which no study has yet compared systematically. This paper codes the public rule pages of 40 firms, observed on 5 May 2026, along eleven dimensions covering evaluation parameters and rules that bear on automated and replicated trading. Three findings stand out. First, headline parameters are strikingly uniform: a 5% daily and 10% maximum loss limit, an 80% base profit split, no time limit and MetaTrader connectivity each appear at a majority of firms, with 23 of 40 firms offering MetaTrader and nothing else. Second, the rules that matter most to algorithmic traders are the least documented: automated strategies are permitted in some form at 39 firms, yet an explicit public rule on copy trading was found at only six, every one of which confines copying to the trader's own accounts. Third, 27% of all rule statements are conditional on the programme chosen or otherwise indeterminate, and the median firm has three such rules. The paper argues that the combination of uniform headline terms and opaque conduct rules shifts risk onto the trader at payout time and bears directly on the regulatory question of whether evaluation fees purchase a service whose terms can be known in advance. The dataset is open.

detail.abstract: Responsible artificial intelligence (RAI) frameworks have converged around governance dimensions-fairness, transparency, accountability, safety, and privacy-while treating the environmental resource cost of AI systems as a separate, largely voluntary concern housed in corporate sustainability or ESG reporting rather than in AI governance itself. This paper argues that the separation is a category error rather than a neutral division of labor. Drawing on distributive-justice, harm-based, and systemic-risk reasoning, we contend that the energy, water, and material footprint of AI development and deployment is properly a responsible-AI concern. We further argue that a significant share of this footprint is generated not by genuine use-case need but by mimetic adoption, formalized here through institutional-isomorphism theory and the construct of AI-specific "FOMO Pressure". Beyond the normative argument, this paper contributes a technical artifact: a computational framework for real-time, per-prompt estimation of the energy, water, and carbon footprint of large language model (LLM) inference, including an explicit treatment of agentic, multi-step workloads grounded in recent infrastructure-level measurements. We present the system architecture, the underlying mathematical model (single-turn energy, uncertainty quantification, water-use-effectiveness translation, carbon translation, and an agentic step-tier extension), and an illustrative worked comparison across seven representative model configurations. We then reframe pragmatic, use-case-driven deployment as the mechanism by which sustainability and responsible AI converge, and we propose a four-gate integration pathway-use-case justification, lifecycle disclosure, procurement-linked accountability, and design-stage incentives-that treats both restraint and measurement as governance requirements rather than public-relations features.

detail.abstract: We study differences in economic outcomes by perceived skin tone among African Americans using full-count U.S. decennial census data from the late-19 th and early-20 th centuries. Comparing children coded as "Black" or "Mulatto" by census enumerators and linking these children across population censuses, we first document large gaps in educational attainment and income among African Americans with darker and lighter perceived skin tones. To disentangle the drivers of these gaps, we identify all 35, 992 families in which enumerators assigned same-gender siblings different Black/Mulatto classifications. Relative to sisters coded as Mulatto, sisters coded as Black had lower educational attainment, were less likely to marry, and had less-educated, likely lower-earning husbands. These patterns are consistent with more severe contemporaneous discrimination against African American women with darker perceived skin tones. In contrast, we find similar educational attainment, marital outcomes, and incomes among differently-classified brothers. Men perceived as African Americans of any skin tone faced similar contemporaneous discrimination, consistent with the "one-drop" racial classification rule that grouped together individuals with any known Black ancestry. Lower incomes for African American men perceived as having darker skin tone in the general population were driven by differences in opportunities and resources that varied across families, likely reflecting the impacts of historical or family-level discrimination.

detail.abstract: Integrated AI-enabled decision-support systems are developing mainly by increasing data volume, processing speed, computing power, depth of automation and decision tempo. Under an uncorrected systematic error, faster decision cycles can increase deviation and push the system beyond its stability boundary. Public and professional descriptions directly equate these improvements with better management, and the dominant OODA-loop doctrine holds that whoever completes the decision cycle faster wins. The limits of this approach are examined on a model of the closed management loop: environment → goal → data collection → processing → decision → action → changed environment. Two propositions are substantiated. First, improving one link of a closed loop does not eliminate the problem but causes its migration in one of three forms: it reveals or shifts the bottleneck, amplifies a pre-existing weakness, or creates a new problem through the very way the original one was solved. Second, increasing the cycle frequency under an uncorrected systematic error increases the deviation over the same calendar time; a deviation of 1% per cycle yields +48.9% or -33.1% after 40 cycles. This holds for an error that arises with every decision; an error proportional to the step length is not amplified by acceleration, and it is the distinction between these two classes that determines whether acceleration helps or harms. A model with correction and feedback delay shows that without retuning, acceleration drives the system beyond its stability boundary, up to the destruction of its function, and that even under optimal tuning there is an interior optimum of frequency: the optimal cycle length is of the order of the feedback delay, and deciding more often than the environment responds to previous decisions is harmful. It follows that one should seek not the maximum of local parameters but their dynamic optimum, and reallocate resources to finding it. As a practical consequence, the Adaptive Staircase is proposed: management of the trajectory of change (timing of introduction, duration and sequence of decisions), including the cost of a competitor's adaptation in a shared environment. Palantir-type systems serve as the best-documented example of the class of AI-enabled decision-support systems (AI-DSS).

detail.abstract: This paper reports a precision audit of a production filter stack against a 13-day window of post-rejection forward-market observations on Solana DEX trading (2026-04-10 to 2026-04-23, UTC). The audit yielded 99,510 follow-up samples across 2,402 unique rejection events spanning eight active filter rules. The descriptive result is a save-to-miss ratio of 3.7 : 1 (418 windowed measured-drawdown saves against 112 misses). This ratio is a descriptive count, not by itself evidence of filter skill: a fair-game price path also reaches a 50 percent drawdown before a 100 percent rise more often than the reverse, and a rebuilt analysis supersedes it. Correction (October 2026): I withdraw the early-death tier, the wider 14.8 : 1 ratio that rested on it, and the matched lifecycle comparison (48.9 versus 57.6 percent of mints reaching the gone state). I also withdraw the claim that every adequately sampled filter is individually net-positive (filter_7 has 3 saves and 3 misses). Per-filter estimates may be affected because follow-up records are keyed by token rather than by rejection decision. Details are in the correction notice on page 1.

detail.abstract: To study monetary policy transmission at the firm level, researchers typically consider heterogeneity along a small number of firm characteristics, such as size or leverage. We instead estimate the full distribution of firms' investment responses to monetary policy, using a clustering regression framework. Our novel approach captures multidimensional and unobservable heterogeneity across firms and time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. Only about 5 percent of firm-time observations are associated with a strong response. We then investigate the sources of heterogeneity ex post. We find that most of the variation in investment sensitivity arises within firms over time. Although several firm characteristics predict responsiveness to monetary policy, the majority of heterogeneity remains unexplained by firm observables. We demonstrate that our empirical estimates provide new targets for disciplining structural models of firm heterogeneity.

detail.abstract: Bayesian spatial survival models for tuberculosis (TB) usually combine a district-level random effect with a linear predictor, so nonlinear covariate effects must be specified by hand, and machine-learning survival models usually ignore spatial dependence and report no parameter uncertainty. No published method links the two for in-hospital outcomes of TB patients, and the three-parameter Dagum distribution, whose hazard can rise and then fall, has not been used for this endpoint. We present a three-stage method that fills this gap. First, a random survival forest (RSF) compresses 25 admission-time predictors into a scalar risk index, computed by cross-fitting so that no patient’s index is learned from that patient’s own outcome. Second, the index enters the log-scale of a Dagum accelerated failure time model with a proper conditional autoregressive (CAR) district effect whose full density, including the determinant term, is used during sampling. Third, the hybrid model and simpler alternatives are validated on patients held out before any fitting. The method was demonstrated on 223 patients from one hospital in Tuban Regency, Indonesia (20 districts, 2025), with discharge with clinical improvement as the event. On the held-out patients, Harrell’s C-index was 0.627 (95% CI 0.520–0.733) for the RSF alone and 0.575 (0.457–0.691) for the full hybrid model. The spatial term did not improve discrimination (paired ΔC −0.052, 95% CI −0.167 to 0.054); district effects were small and uncertain, and the Dagum fit was adequate. The method is a reproducible template; code and a synthetic example dataset are provided.

detail.abstract: The term the "Barassi Line" was coined in the 1970s to define the geographical distribution of Australia's football codes. Sports scholars have primarily focused upon empirical studies of club location, participation, resourcing, and spectatorship for Australian rules football versus rugby league, and to a lesser extent rugby union and soccer (association football). Lesser attention has been given to the economic and social influences informing the historical emergence of Australian football geographical concentration. In this paper the early development of Australian football is described with reference to "emergent order" theory, which appraises observed human activities as being derived from a bottom-up process involving economic and social interactions between individuals and groups. This contrasts with arrangements attributable to deliberate efforts by any specific individual or organization. Emergent order theory is applied to analyse the evolution of Australian rules, specifically in a southern New South Wales region known as the Riverina, prior to World War I. Colonial-era migration to the Riverina from areas with strong support for Australian rules football is critical to Barassi Line emergence, as was economic development and civic associational activities. Alternative explanations for the Barassi Line, such as railway construction, are critically assessed.

detail.abstract: This paper tests whether the U.S. options market leads emerging-market equity returns around fifteen selected U.S. tariff and export-control events between January 2018 and April 2025. We build an industry-level skew signal, using option-implied volatility of S&P 1500 companies, and a production-network exposure measure through Leontief propagation across Inter-Country Input-Output tables, tested on 4,693 firms across 25 emerging economies, asking whether a lead exists, whether it scales with a firm's network exposure, and whether it differs for the directly targeted country. The pooled result is marginal, and exposure and target status find nothing at any horizon, an ambiguity that could mean no lead exists, or one hidden by pooling. A deeper look tells a different story, one that hints at co-movement rather than the transmission channel we set out to test.

detail.abstract:
Standards are common platforms that allow products to work together. Sometimes, the owners of patents incorporated into standards receive royalty payments from those adopting the standard. But other times, standards development organizations do not require royalties, instead employing royalty-free licensing. Such licensing “has grown increasingly common,” with “perhaps only a small percentage of today’s widely adopted standards-based technologies . . . subject to royalty payments.”

Despite their prevalence, royalty-free licensing policies have recently been in the crosshairs of the Department of Justice’s (“DOJ”) Antitrust Division. Dina Kallay, a senior DOJ official who just left the agency, claimed that such licensing reflected a closed standard among dominant implementers that collude and reduce innovation.

This essay highlights seven flaws with such a position, focusing on aspects of royalty-free licensing relating to (1) litigation, (2) the growth of the Internet, (3) longstanding history, (4) market benefits, (5) innovation benefits, (6) closed categorization, and (7) bipartisan treatment. The essay also shows how one-sided positions critical of royalty-free licensing threaten to undermine the Administration’s artificial intelligence goals, as reflected in the Executive Office of the President’s action plan and National Institute of Standards and Technology pilot project. Given the chance for a fresh start at the agency with Kallay’s departure, this essay highlights the harms from her position.

detail.abstract: This study compares the effects of carbon pricing and command-and-control regulation on firms' environmental performance. I leverage a unique dual-policy setting in South Korea, where a carbon pricing scheme (the Emissions Trading Scheme, ETS) and a command-and-control program (the Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel. Because each firm is regulated under only one of the two, the setting allows a direct comparison of the two approaches. Using a difference-indifferences design on firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2022, I find that firms that transitioned from the TMS to the ETS reduced energy use by 5.8% to 8.8% and carbon emissions by 7.3% to 8.5% relative to firms that remained under the TMS, while effects on carbon intensity were not robust. Because TMS firms were themselves subject to binding emissions targets, these estimates reflect the additional effect of carbon pricing over command-and-control regulation. The absence of a robust intensity effect indicates that the ETS reduced emissions without a measurable improvement in emissions efficiency. A phase-specific analysis further shows that the reductions were strongest in the more market-oriented phases of the ETS, which featured allowance auctioning and benchmark-based allocation. This suggests that jurisdictions transitioning from command-and-control regulation to carbon pricing can strengthen its effectiveness by phasing in auctioning and benchmark-based allocation rather than relying on free allocation.

detail.abstract: I stress-test an opening-range breakout (ORB) under a validation protocol assembled from established components: a pre-registered ledger of every configuration searched, deflation of the Sharpe ratio against that ledger's own count, walk-forward evaluation with parameters fixed ex ante, two permutation nulls at 5,000 resamples each, and transaction costs measured from a live broker fill. The estimand is narrow and worth naming precisely. Because non-farm payrolls fall on the first Friday of most months and are filtered out along with CPI, FOMC and mega-cap earnings weeks, this is not a generic Friday effect but an event-free Friday effect. On 2018-2026 one-minute bars, a 30-minute ORB restricted to such Fridays earns +0.44R per trade out of sample on QQQ (profit factor 2.77) and +0.31R on SPY (1.95), both clearing a bootstrap null at p < 0.002. Deflating for the study's full ledger of 57 configuration probes, with the trial-dispersion-parameter scaled to the sample as a weekly strategy requires, gives a Deflated Sharpe Ratio of 0.78 on QQQ and 0.42 on SPY; read instead as a clean holdout, the zero-edge probability of the observed out-of-sample Sharpe is 0.002. Both quantities depend on judgements about the search rather than on the data, so I report the range and argue that only a forward test narrows it. Across seventeen instruments the effect concentrates in technology, broad-growth and metals exposures and is absent in defensive and rate-sensitive sectors; nine of seventeen clear both nulls. Because the ORB return stream is essentially uncorrelated with the index (ρ =-0.03), a fixed 50/50 blend of rule and buy-and-hold rebalanced monthly improves on both, raising the QQQ Sharpe ratio from 1.13 and 0.88 to 1.43 and beating the standalone rule in all sixteen instruments the rule trades.

detail.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) pose a critical safety risk in high-stakes domains such as medicine, where a factually incorrect response can have life-threatening consequences. As more people consult LLMs before seeking medical care, hallucinations can result in life-threatening misdiagnoses, incorrect medication recommendations, and unsafe emergency triage, posing a significant risk to patient safety. In this work, we present Hallucination-Aware Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (HA-MedRAG), a two-stage framework that detects and mitigates hallucinations in medical question answering. For detection, we give the medical question as input to the LLM and extract the LLM’s internal signals at the first token generation of the answer, specifically Softmax probability distributions, self-attention scores, and fully-connected (FFN) layer activations from Mistral-7B-Instruct, and train a weighted ensemble classifier over the dataset created from these extracted signals. For mitigation, we introduce a domain-adapted Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that uses UMLS (Unified Medical Language System)-informed query expansion, hybrid dense-sparse retrieval with Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) re-ranking, and fallback to live PubMed Central and Wikipedia sources. The detector is trained and evaluated on 15,177 labeled samples from the medical meadow medical flashcards dataset, with a held-out test set of 2,277 samples. Our proposed technique achieves an AUROC of 0.7242 on the held-out test set, a small but statistically significant improvement over the strongest individual signal-specific classifier (FFN, AUROC 0.7132; paired DeLong p=0.004), while also returning calibrated probability estimates. On 5,000 separate held-out evaluation samples the RAG pipeline lowers the hallucination rate from 15.1% to 12.1%, a relative reduction of 19.8%, and improves accuracy on answered questions from 85.7% to 87.0%. However, this comes at a coverage cost of 6.6%, as the system abstains on some questions, which reduces the number of delivered correct answers by 3.6 percentage points. Our work demonstrates that internal LLM signals, originally studied in open-domain factual QA, transfer meaningfully to the medical domain despite its added lexical and semantic complexity.

detail.abstract: Urban megafires cause catastrophic and enduring losses, as burning structures expose and ignite their neighbors. What degree of structure-to-structure exposure triggers self-sustained fire spread under real-world conditions, however, is not well understood. Here, I construct a Structure-to-Structure Exposure Network by measuring geometric coupling between buildings from LiDAR-derived building meshes to assess post-fire damage for 24,771 exposed structures assessed within the perimeters of the 2025 Los Angeles fires. Destruction increased nonlinearly with exposure intensity, as tolerance of hardened building assemblies weakened. Using fire progression reconstruction and an instrumental-variable strategy, I find documented structure-defense actions reduced destruction for targeted structures and down-fire neighbors, consistent with defense removing potential sources of heat and embers. Finally, applying these empirical thresholds in a forward-looking risk assessment identifies at-risk communities across California, where reducing structure-to-structure connectivity may provide greater fire resilience than parcel-level hardening alone.

detail.abstract: Rising top income shares predict financial crises, but the mechanisms behind this relationship are not fully understood. We provide evidence for a novel channel through which this relationship may operate: bank funding. Using U.S. bank-level data (1985-2022), we find that a rise in the top 1% income share reduces core deposits and increases noncore funding share of banks, while gains among the 90th-99th percentiles have opposite effects. These patterns are consistent with differences in household portfolio allocation across the income distribution. As banks substitute toward noncore deposits and wholesale funding, their funding fragility increases. Top income concentration also predicts higher subsequent bank failure risk, with about one-third accounted for by changes in funding structure.

detail.abstract: More than seven million Venezuelans now live outside Venezuela, and nearly every legal status they seek abroad depends on the same small set of Venezuelan documents: the identity card, the passport, the civil registry certificate, and the criminal record certificate. The documents travel; the methods used to verify them do not. This paper compares how five host jurisdictions that together receive the majority of the Venezuelan diaspora, namely the United States, Spain, Colombia, Chile, and Peru, authenticate and weigh Venezuelan documents in immigration, protection, and regularization proceedings. It identifies five distinct verification models: adversarial evidentiary weighing (United States), administrative documentary formalism (Spain), biometric registry substitution (Colombia), consular pre-screening (Chile), and intelligence-led enforcement (Peru). Drawing on the author's experience as a former Venezuelan organized crime prosecutor, the paper shows that each model fails in a predictable direction. Some systems admit forged or misleading documents that carry a valid apostille (false negatives), while others reject genuine documents because they are expired, non-standard, or impossible to obtain from a collapsed consular network (false positives). The paper isolates five structural vulnerabilities that transnational criminal organizations, including the Tren de Aragua, can exploit, chief among them the widespread misreading of the Venezuelan criminal record certificate as proof of a clean history. It closes with a five-layer Multinational Verification Protocol and policy recommendations for adjudicators, governments, and expert witnesses. Declaration of Generative AI Use. detail.abstract: Textbooks present the free-rider problem as a failure of demand revelation: at their given incomes, people understate what public goods are worth to them. A parallel failure is rarely taught, primarily because it is a relatively new observation, not because it is a difficult concept. People earn income in order to buy things, and no one can individually buy more police protection, cleaner air, or a safer climate, so the income that would have been spent on such goods is never earned, introducing distortions in the markets for substitute and complement goods. This article offers three short, self-contained teaching modules built on that observation. The first, for principles courses, uses public safety to show that under-provided public goods reduce work effort and shift spending toward private substitutes (locks, alarms, large private yards) and away from private complements. The second, for intermediate microeconomics and environmental economics, starts from Samuelson's treatment of inputs as negative outputs, introduces "supply revelation" as the input-market counterpart of demand revelation, and shows why valuations that hold hours of work fixed understate the benefits of public-good increments. The third, for urban economics, uses the argument to explain why suburbanization has been excessive.

detail.abstract:
Purpose. 
A firm's multi-agent AI system approves a loan, escalates a support ticket, or rewrites a block of production code, with no human reviewing the intermediate steps. When something goes wrong, the postmortem runs into a wall: the output was the joint product of several interacting agents, none of whom made a decision in the way the organization's accountability structures expect. This paper examines why existing governance frameworks fail to answer a basic question in this setting, who is responsible, and proposes a framework that locates where that failure concentrates and why. 
Design/methodology/approach. 
This is a conceptual paper. It synthesizes the technical literature on agentic AI security, coordination, and evaluation, and extends three established organizational theories (IT governance decision-rights theory, agency theory, and sociotechnical systems theory) into the multi-agent context. The resulting framework crosses decision stakes (routine, exceptional, strategic) against agent architecture (single-agent, human-supervised multi-agent, autonomous multi-agent) to identify where responsibility attribution is most likely to break down.
Findings. 
The dominant literature on agentic AI treats accountability primarily as a technical logging problem, to be solved with better audit trails and more interpretable model outputs. That is necessary but not sufficient. Responsibility attribution is fundamentally a decision-rights problem, and the highest-risk zone, exceptional and strategic decisions handled by autonomous multi-agent systems, is also the zone organizations are most eager to automate, because it is the most expensive to review with humans at scale. Three governance mechanisms follow from the framework: agent-level provenance tracking at each delegation handoff, escalation rules tied to decision type rather than model confidence, and organizational roles built specifically to interpret what the agents did. 
Practical implications.
The framework gives compliance and internal audit functions a diagnostic for locating their own deployments on the risk grid and checking whether governance mechanisms match the risk level present. It also gives IT governance committees a vocabulary, agent authority scope, for a decision domain that current frameworks do not yet name. 
Originality/value
Existing work on responsibility in agentic AI is either technical, focused on logging and interpretability, or normative and legal, focused on what should happen in principle. This paper extends established IT governance and decision-rights theory to the emerging context of  enterprise multi-agent AI systems. The paper closes with a case for testing this framework against real deployments, through interviews with the people currently living inside this problem.

detail.abstract: Corporate governance is the system by which companies are controlled and accountability structures and processes are imposed on those in control of companies. In the wake of financial crises, in 1999 the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) devised the Principles of Corporate Governance. The OECD Principles of Corporate Governance is an answer to a global search for optimal corporate governance standards. Governments value good corporate governance, because it contributes to the attractiveness of local companies for foreign investment. Companies value optimal corporate governance, because it drives positive stock performance. While the principles are a widely accepted global model, they are not necessarily what determine successful corporate governance. As Subramanian (2015) explained in his article “Corporate Governance 2.0,” there is a lack of an accepted metric on what constitutes such success. As the OECD continues to revise through each edition, this book chapter explains two aspects of the review and revision, namely family businesses and climate change governance.

detail.abstract: Firms and researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to turn unstructured regulatory disclosures into structured variables, but the reliability of these model-generated measurements is rarely checked before the outputs are used. We evaluate 11 LLMs (three proprietary API models and eight openweight models of 7B to 32B parameters, including reasoning and non-reasoning variants) on a common structured-extraction task applied to 35 Item 1A "Risk Factors" sections from U.S. public companies' SEC 10-K filings. The task has three nested sub-tasks of increasing granularity: extracting discrete risk factors, classifying each into a fixed nine-category taxonomy, and scoring each on three 1-10 dimensions (financial impact, likelihood, urgency). We apply a two-layer reliability protocol: first whether a model returns a schema-valid output, then, conditional on valid output, how stable it is across repetitions (ICC) and how much models agree; we also add a human-annotated validity spot-check of 62 extracted risks. Three results stand out. Reliability depends strongly on how fine-grained the judgment is: cross-model classification agreement (0.72) is higher than scoring rank-agreement (Spearman 0.57), which in turn is higher than extraction overlap (Jaccard 0.44), and even the most stable proprietary model reaches only ICC ≈ 0.89 on scoring. Reasoning-tuned open models are less reliable on both layers; they more often fail to return valid output, and their scores vary far more across repetitions (mean scoring ICC 0.36 versus 0.70 for nonreasoning models; difference 0.33, 95% CI [0.30, 0.37]). The validity check follows the same ordering: extraction precision is high (1.00), classification accuracy moderate (0.92), and score plausibility lowest (0.87). We describe the procedure as a reusable reliability-and-validity audit and recommend that studies report both for the specific sub-task they rely on, rather than treating fluent output as evidence of a sound measurement.

LendingClub loan data have been combined with macroeconomic variables from FRED, whereas FDIC financial data have been used for institution-level analysis. Dif erent algorithms such as logistic regression, random forest, LightGBM, XGBoost, and deep neural network were assessed using chronological training, validation, and testing samples. XGBoost demonstrated the best results in terms of performance on a borrower level with 0.7197 and 0.7139 ROC-AUC scores on the validation and testing samples, correspondingly. The deep neural network generated similar discriminatory power but had lower specificity and more false positives. Multi-task LSTM was implemented to forecast the equity-to-assets ratio four quarters ahead and performed better than the benchmark model.The techniques SHAP and LIME recognized interest rate, FICO score, level of indebtedness, loan term, homeownership, and macroeconomic environment as key determinants that af ect credit risk prediction. Stress testing of the macroeconomic environment determined which borrowers are sensitive to negative scenarios, and the agentic reporting layer created structured reports for borrowers, explanations, stress test results, and human review flags. In general, the results show that the combination of predictive modelling, explainability, stress testing, and human review is possible.

detail.abstract:
Generative AI has evolved rapidly in the last few years and has made an impact across many areas of cognitive work. While the adoption in the technical work has clearly demonstrated the advantages of automation, the impact on managerial work effective ness is relatively less understood. Existing research operationalizes effectiveness through task level efficiency. Product Managers’ roles in software companies, especially in an emerging market like India, are not task-oriented and mostly depend on human judgement.  
This study examined the impact of GenAI adoption on the effectiveness of product managers in early-stage SaaS companies in India and whether experience or team size moderates that impact. Effectiveness was decomposed into three product life cycle stages – discovery, development and go-to-market. The study adopted a positivist philosophy with deductive approach and used cross-sectional survey data from 93 product managers. These data were analysed using PLS-SEM with significance assessed through bootstrapping.  
The study had twenty-one hypotheses and all of which were rejected. This means that, in the sample, GenAI adoption did not enhance the effectiveness of product managers and the moderating effects of experience and team size were not significant. The study, however, revealed a new construct ‘AI augmented Judgement,’ operationalised as ability to interpret, evaluate and integrate the AI output, which predicted five of the six outcomes. The largest effects were found on cycle time & quality during development phase. This construct emerged distinct from experience and its effect was additive rather than multiplicative as originally hypothesized.  
The study concluded that GenAI adoption is already commoditised and hence it is no longer the differentiator. However, the judgement required to convert the probabilistic outcomes into product decisions is the real differentiator. This carries an implication for product managers and leaders on how GenAI tools should be embraced within the organisation for maximum effectiveness.

detail.abstract: Production AI systems deployed in high-stakes domains accumulate a governance liability that existing monitoring frameworks fail to detect: the progressive inability to explain individual decisions when regulators, auditors, or affected individuals demand accountability. We introduce TRACE (Transparency, Risk, Accountability, Compliance, and Explainability), a seven-instrument governance framework for measuring, tracking, and remediating Explainability Debt in production AI systems. The foundational instrument, the Explainability Debt Score (EDS), quantifies the proportion of production decisions falling below a governance-defined explainability confidence threshold at any point in time. Complementary instruments include DART (Debt Accumulation Rate Tracker for breach forecasting), SHIV (Scenario Health and Integrity Validator for daily governance), FDE (Feature Drift Evaluator for causal attribution), HVE (Human Validation Engine), AIDE (Audit Intervention Decision Engine), and ZERO (Zero Explainability Risk Optimiser for remediation). Through a twelve-month longitudinal case study of a production fraud detection system processing 50,000 daily financial transactions, achieving 98.46% accuracy and ROC-AUC of 0.9990, we demonstrate that an EDS of 0.23 on audit day was statistically predictable six months in advance using DART trajectory analysis (beta = 0.008/week, R-squared = 0.94, 95% CI: [0.006, 0.010]), and that 78% of Explainability Debt was concentrated in the highest-regulatoryrisk decision category (transactions above $10,000), a risk asymmetry completely invisible to systemlevel metrics. TRACE provides the first quantitative operational architecture for EU AI Act Article 13 compliance in production AI deployment, establishing a new subdiscipline of explanation governance distinct from explanation generation.

detail.abstract: The transition from generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes the analytical problem of the future of work. Earlier automation research largely asked whether machines could perform particular tasks; current agentic systems add planning, tool use, memory, delegation, and multi-step execution, making it possible for a software system to occupy a more persistent position inside an organizational workflow. This systematic review synthesizes recent empirical, theoretical, and policy evidence on the emergence of AI agents as a prospective digital workforce and asks whether "AI as a workforce" is a meaningful analytical category rather than a rhetorical metaphor. Following PRISMAinformed procedures and a transparent multidisciplinary search protocol, the review integrates peerreviewed studies, working papers, large-scale labor-market datasets, and authoritative institutional reports published principally between 2018 and October 2026, with foundational work retained where theoretically indispensable. The synthesis identifies five recurring mechanisms: task substitution, task augmentation, coordination automation, new-task creation, and redistribution of human agency. Empirical evidence shows substantial productivity gains in bounded knowledge tasks, heterogeneous effects by worker skill and task type, and early evidence of task reorganization rather than immediate aggregate employment collapse. The World Economic Forum projects 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced by 2030 across major macrotrends, while the International Labour Organization estimates that about one quarter of global employment is potentially exposed to GenAI, emphasizing that exposure is not a forecast of job loss. More recent agentic-AI scholarship suggests that autonomy itself becomes an organizational resource and risk. The review develops a novel "Agentic Workforce Transition" framework in which AI agents are treated as quasi-organizational actors whose economic effects depend on capability, autonomy, organizational embedding, and governance. The central critical proposition is an Agency Paradox: increasing machine autonomy may increase, rather than eliminate, the demand for human judgment, accountability, and system-level supervision-while simultaneously hollowing out the task-level experience through which expertise is traditionally acquired.

detail.abstract:
​Background: The European Health Data Space (EHDS) requires adaptation of healthcare systems and workforce readiness. However, evidence on competency gaps across Europe remains limited. This study aimed to establish a baseline of workforce readiness and prioritise interoperability gaps relevant to EHDS implementation, through a multi-stakeholder survey conducted within the Xpanding Innovative Alliance (XiA) project.

Methods: A cross-sectional needs assessment survey was conducted among 359 respondents from 23 European countries. Participants rated their current skill proficiency and development needs across 28 digital skills and 13 digital health standard domains, alongside training delivery and certification requirements. Competency gaps were evaluated using descriptive and composite measures, including Borich Mean Weighted Discrepancy Score (MWDS). Non-parametric inferential analysis and linear regression examined the relationship between skills and needs, while Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests assessed variance across background variables. Priority domains were identified using non-parametric bootstrapping.

Findings: The analysis revealed significant competency gaps across all tested domains. These deficits were primarily skill-driven, with a strong inverse correlation between skill level and gap magnitude. AI and Machine Learning in Healthcare emerged as the highest priority domain (MWDS of 2.20), followed by Ethical Frameworks for AI (MWDS of 1.97) and e-health data standards (MWDS of 1.63). Digital maturity varied significantly by profession and country, while institution type did not significantly impact perceived future needs. Online self-paced learning was the preferred delivery mode. Certification requirements differed significantly by country and institution.

Interpretation: Substantial competency gaps exist across the EHDS ecosystem, with larger gaps observed among professionals reporting lower levels of digital competency.  Differences across professions and roles support a role-based approach to upskilling, while the high demand for AI/ML, ethics, and interoperability standards highlights priority areas for training. Preferences for flexible online training further support a continuous and adaptable approach to workforce development. These findings provide an evidence base for developing European curricula to support EHDS workforce readiness.

detail.abstract: Generative AI now makes responsiveness and privilege determinations in live litigation. detail.abstract: Heat of combustion is an important thermochemical property for evaluating organic compounds, fuels, energetic materials, and energy-related applications. Accurate prediction of this property can support chemical screening while reducing dependence on time-consuming experimental measurements. This study investigates the application of quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) and machinelearning techniques to predict the heat of combustion of organic compounds from molecular structures and calculated molecular descriptors. The research involves dataset preparation, molecular descriptor generation and selection, model development, training and testing, statistical validation, comparison of machine-learning algorithms, and interpretation of influential molecular features. Among the evaluated models, the Random Forest model using molecular descriptors produced the strongest predictive performance, with an R² of 0.9927, RMSE of 342.0464 kJ mol⁻¹, and MAE of 142.2272 kJ mol⁻¹. The findings demonstrate the potential of QSPR and machine learning as rapid complementary approaches to experimental thermochemical determination, while emphasizing that prediction reliability depends on dataset quality, molecular diversity, descriptor selection, and appropriate external validation

detail.abstract: Most conversations about improving operations in Mexico start and end with standards: ISO 9001, IATF 16949, Lean, Six Sigma. Those standards are useful, and I have spent years applying them. But a standard only describes what a good process should look like. People are the ones who run it, and people bring their culture to work with them. In this essay I argue, from more than twelve years in manufacturing, logistics, quality, and trade, that culture is the variable we talk about least and that costs us the most, particularly in Mexican plants and warehouses owned by European, Canadian, and American investors. I describe four situations I have seen repeat themselves: audits that are passed on paper and ignored on the floor; direct feedback that local teams receive as public humiliation; data-driven management that never takes root because it is taught in a conference room instead of on the line; and a courteous management style that hides poor performance until someone is fired for it. For each one, I connect what I saw with published research on national culture, employee voice, feedback, leadership, and training. The practical answer I propose rests on two ideas. Keep the requirement of the standard, but adapt the mechanism. And give the people who understand both cultures, the "local eyes," a real role in deciding how. I close with a short list of questions that a board should be asking before it signs a nearshoring deal.

detail.abstract: Developers of large language models license human-written content to train their models, while users increasingly produce content with these models. In a dynamic model of the market for training data, a better model attracts more users, increasing the value of better performance but also raising the share of generated content in future data sources. Much of this content echoes what the model already knows and concentrates on common tasks, reducing both the information and the task diversity contained in the data. We show that information dilution alone causes the value of a data source to decline gradually, whereas the loss of task coverage can produce a market freeze. Once the generated share crosses a threshold, developers stop buying from the data pool even at a zero price, possibly while most records are human, while verified data become relatively more valuable. Successful AI can therefore reverse the usual positive data network effect because greater adoption can reduce the value of the data available to train future models. Market freezes are temporary as knowledge depreciates and adoption falls, but strong feedback between model performance and data quality can destabilize the steady state and generate recurring booms and freezes. Certifying informational provenance, meaning whether a record contains observations beyond existing model knowledge, eliminates the freeze. By contrast, information about who or what produced a record provides only an imperfect signal of its informational value. Information about record origin and task coverage can each restore trade, and the two can be complements.

detail.abstract: Investors who hold gold through online platforms almost universally evaluate their position by a single observable: the quoted price of the metal. This paper argues that the quoted price systematically under-describes the risk actually borne, and that the omitted component, platform risk, is not a rounding error but frequently the dominant term in the holder's return distribution. I decompose a client's realised return into a commodity term, a structural claim term, tracking error, fee drag, a credit term and a liquidity term, of which only the first is priced by the market. I introduce two analytical constructs: the Metal-Claim Ladder, a continuum of gold exposures ranked by claim quality rather than by asset class, and the Claim-Adjusted Cost of Exposure (CACE), which restates platform risk as an annualised basis-point charge commensurable with visible fees. I show that an unallocated or pooled gold balance is economically a risky claim on the operator's balance sheet, that the embedded redemption right is an option whose value depends on the operator's funding structure, and that instant-withdrawal promises against physically settled metal constitute a maturity transformation with the run surface documented for money market and bond funds. Finally, I map these mechanisms onto four supervisory instruments (BCBS d516, DORA, NIST CSF 2.0 and the FSB's work on technology and financial stability) and propose a minimal disclosure set that makes platform risk legible to ordinary users. The paper is conceptual and normative; it uses no proprietary or empirical data, and the author's conflict of interest is disclosed.

detail.abstract:
The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-generated information within justice systems has intensified questions concerning evidentiary reliability, authenticity, human oversight, and institutional accountability. As the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules prepares to revisit proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 and potential amendments to Rule 901 on October 15, 2026, the legal system is confronting how AI-generated evidence should be evaluated. However, a critical governance question remains insufficiently addressed: What happens after technology-generated information enters the human decision-making process?

This paper examines the distinction between technical reliability, evidentiary admissibility, and human decision accountability. It introduces the Decision Visibility Gap, a condition in which institutions preserve technology outputs and resulting actions but lack sufficient evidence to reconstruct how human decision-makers received, interpreted, verified, relied upon, and acted on that information.

Drawing upon scholarship concerning automation bias, algorithmic accountability, human oversight, and sociotechnical governance, the paper presents Justice Decision Observability (JDO), an independent governance and decision-evidence framework developed by Justice Beacon Solutions (JBS). 

Through hypothetical applications involving law enforcement, correctional operations, and community supervision, the analysis demonstrates how technically reliable outputs may coexist with incomplete human decision records. It further distinguishes evidence-centered governance from traditional technology audits, compliance assessments, and employee evaluations.

This study aims to develop molecular structure-based models for predicting enthalpy of combustion and related thermodynamic properties using molecular structure-derived descriptors and statistical or machine-learning techniques. A dataset of compounds with experimentally reported thermodynamic properties will be compiled, molecular descriptors will be calculated, and relevant features will be selected before model development and validation. The best-performing model, identified using independent statistical evaluation, will be reported using its coefficient of determination (R²), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE), together with the descriptors that contribute most strongly to prediction. The findings are expected to demonstrate the potential of molecular structurebased modelling as a practical computational approach for thermodynamic prediction and molecular screening.

title: Anthrobud Theory: A Developmental Framework for Emerging Structures of Humanity and Early-Stage Forecasting

detail.title: Anthrobud Theory: A Developmental Framework for Emerging Structures of Humanity and Early-Stage Forecasting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Forecasting consequential technological developments at an early stage is difficult because novelty, rapid change, uncertain applications, incomplete markets, evolving institutions, and unresolved constraints weaken conventional extrapolation. Existing literatures illuminate important parts of this problem but typically take technologies, ventures, readiness levels, innovation systems, or diffusion curves as the focal object. This paper introduces Anthrobud Theory, which makes the emerging developmental structure itself explicit within the evolving structure of humanity: a newly germinated configuration in which scientific, technological, social, cultural, organizational, and/or institutional elements begin to cohere into a new capability or configuration with substantial but materially uncertain future potential for incorporation into humanity's established structure. The framework characterizes an Anthrobud through Value, Vigor, Scope, Resources, and Resistance (VVSRR), defines Anthrobud Value (AV) as a point-in-time estimate of development-based value, and defines Anthrobud Value Gain (AVG) as its change over a stated period. When sufficient VVSRR evidence is available, AV and AVG can support value assessment before public listing and distinguish development-based from market-based valuation after listing. A 19-technology benchmark evaluates an observable trajectory subset across 57 three-year-ahead forecasts. The Anthrobud trajectory signal is competitive with established diffusion models, while a Gompertz-plus-Anthrobud hybrid achieves the lowest overall RMS log error. A separate 30-venture benchmark uses market capitalization only as a disclosed proxy for AV. Annual proxy AVG (pAVG_t = MC_t-MC_{t-1}), estimated using a sign-preserving asinh transformation, produces the lowest three-year RMSLE (0.474) for revenue prediction among the principal venture specifications. The findings support a bounded interpretation: Anthrobud Theory provides a developmental architecture for forecasting, value assessment, and decision support, with AV, AVG, and trajectory measures serving distinct but complementary roles in understanding and managing emerging structures as they develop toward possible incorporation into humanity's established structure.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the financial policy of stablecoin issuers: how they are funded and how they distribute reserves. We document that issuers with similar business activities may adopt similar policies (MakerDAO and Aave) or very different ones (Tether and Circle). We rationalize this pattern with a model in which the return earned on reserves is a fundamental characteristic that differs between on-chain and off-chain issuers. The higher return available to off-chain issuers exacerbates agency frictions and, in turn, shapes optimal financial policy. We show that the resulting effect is non-monotone in observable outcomes: a higher return can lead to concentrated insider ownership and flexible, aggressive payouts, but it can also lead to dispersed equity ownership and rigid, conservative policies. We close with novel evidence that the implementation of on-chain buyback programs can create stability risks and temporary mispricing.

detail.abstract: China suspended six export-control announcements through an instrument that expires on 10 November 2026. The suspending text is one operative sentence with no conditions, review clause, extension mechanism or reversion procedure. The April 2025 element controls were never suspended. On 23 September 2026, the United States announced a trade-truce extension to 10 January 2027. The six suspended announcements revive on 11 November 2026 unless China publishes an instrument; the September announcement is not one. The 0.1 per cent value threshold and the technology-derived rule in Announcement No. 61 of 2025 have never operated. The suspension period coincided with a State Council supply-chain regulation, a thirteen-category reporting regime and nine entity-list actions. Boards with rare-earth exposure face a documentation deadline rather than a forecasting problem, and the September announcement does not move that deadline until a Chinese instrument does. No valuation methodology, licensing practice or body of ministry decisions exists for the threshold that would commence. The findings bear on Group Procurement Directors in defence manufacturing.

title: Workforce Turnover and Retention in the Public Sector: Insights from Public Pension Plans
affiliations: National Institute on Retirement Security and National Institute on Retirement Security

detail.title: Workforce Turnover and Retention in the Public Sector: Insights from Public Pension Plans

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
This report examines workforce turnover and retention in the public sector using turnover assumptions published in actuarial reports and other information collected from 136 state-administered public pension plans, representing 203 plan-employee groups and 12.8 million active members. The analysis describes how retention varies over employees' careers and across workforce and pension plan characteristics.

The findings show that turnover is concentrated in the early years of employment, with only 48 percent of new hires expected to remain through five years of service. Retention stabilizes considerably thereafter. Among employees who reach five years of service, 53 percent are expected to remain through year 20 and 45 percent through year 30. Retention is generally higher among police and fire employees and teachers than among general, state, and local employees. Retention also varies by pension plan type and Social Security coverage, but differs relatively little by vesting period. Substantial variation across individual plans remains even within employee groups.

These descriptive findings provide new evidence on public-sector employment patterns and offer a framework for comparing retention across pension systems and assessing workforce challenges at different career stages.

detail.abstract: Investors choose not only how much information to acquire, but also how predictive information is represented for decisions. This paper studies how signal form affects portfolio value. In a mean-variance problem, we consider binary tail-event, ternary range, and continuous level signals, with tail and range boundaries determined endogenously. Optimal signal boundaries may shift away from the prior mean toward more extreme return regions, revealing an exploratory feature of information design that generates more valuable posterior portfolio opportunities. Using LLM-based information extraction in commodity futures markets, we show through alternative prompts that the value of information depends not only on predictive content, but also on how it is represented for subsequent decisions.

detail.abstract:
Background: Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) in children under 5 years represent a high-risk area for inappropriate antibiotic use. However, relevant research lacks systematic characterisation of the complete pathway from symptom onset to clinical antibiotic prescription and assessment of pathway-level interventions on prescribing appropriateness.

Methods: We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional survey of children under 5 years with ARIs.. Caregiver-reported data were collected via structured questionnaires. A Bayesian Markov chain model was constructed to simulate care-seeking pathway, calculate state transition probabilities, identify high-risk pathways, and evaluate the impact of four macro-level interventions on inappropriate antibiotic prescribing rates in mild and severe groups.

Results: A total of 2,572 children were enrolled, with 75.8% classified as non-severe and 24.2% as severe. The overall antibiotic prescribing rate was 50.0%, with inappropriate use accounting for 47.1% of all prescriptions. The Markov chain model demonstrated excellent fit (severe group r = 0.996; non-severe group r = 0.980). High-risk pathways, defined by presentation at a high‑level facility without diagnostic testing, were identified in both groups. Counterfactual simulations revealed that all four interventions reduced inappropriate prescribing in non-severe cases. In severe cases, however, lowering first-visit care level and reducing infection frequency paradoxically increased inappropriate use. Mandating in-hospital diagnostic testing was the most powerful and consistent intervention across both groups. 

Conclusions: With half of antibiotic prescriptions inappropriate in children under 5, policy should prioritise high-risk pathways—high-level care without testing. Counterfactuals show mild cases benefit from primary care referral; severe cases require mandatory diagnostics. Stratified, pathway-targeted interventions are essential to curb overuse.
