detail.abstract: When a proposed rule becomes final, what happens to the discrete obligations it contains? This paper aims to introduce a computational method for tracking how individual regulatory obligations survive and transform between proposal and finalization. Applying an extraction pipeline to 870,714 Federal Register documents and a deposited classification set drawn from 21,283 proposed-to-final pairs, I find that the central result is a shape and not a rate. Obligations are overwhelmingly either preserved or eliminated. They are seldom revised. Within the sample, the instrument recognizes 60.2% of proposed-obligation observations as surviving to the final rule in some recognizable form. Roughly two in five have no recognized final-rule counterpart. The observed distribution has but a sliver of a middle ground in that recognized modification and splitting together account for about a tenth of outcomes.

title: Bounding Human Effort in Augmented Intelligence Systems
affiliations: Cornell University, Wisconsin School of Business, Texas A&M University and Pinterest

detail.title: Bounding Human Effort in Augmented Intelligence Systems

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper

affiliations.org_name: University of Wisconsin-Madison - School of Business

detail.abstract: Augmented intelligence systems leverage human-algorithm collaboration to improve decisionmaking in various settings. The performance of such systems hinges on both the algorithm's accuracy and the effort required by humans to correct the algorithm's mistakes. Yet, human correction effort has been ignored in the design of augmented intelligence systems thus far. In this work, we propose a framework that provably endows algorithms in augmented intelligence systems with bounds on the expected human effort required to correct their mistakes. We collaborate with a large social media firm to expand their advertising interest taxonomy using augmented intelligence, and show that bounding human correction effort (keeping algorithmic accuracy fixed) significantly improves the performance of the augmented intelligence system overall by increasing taxonomists' decision-making speed and accuracy. More generally, our research reveals a novel human-centric dimension of optimization for the imperfect algorithms commonly embedded in augmented intelligence systems.

title: The Balancing Pair: Reciprocity of Balancing Measures in Healthcare Quality Indicator Sets under the IHI Model for Improvement and JCI Accreditation Standards ("Baqir's Effect")
affiliations: OMAC International

detail.title: The Balancing Pair: Reciprocity of Balancing Measures in Healthcare Quality Indicator Sets under the IHI Model for Improvement and JCI Accreditation Standards ("Baqir's Effect")

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; the paper is conceptual, uses only hypothetical illustrative data, and involves no patients or human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) Model for Improvement recommends that every improvement effort be tracked with a balanced set of outcome, process, and balancing measures, where balancing measures look at a system from different directions in order to detect unintended consequences of change. Hospitals working under Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation standards, which require leaders to choose what is measured and to act on the results, often carry this guidance into indicator registers as a fixed label: a given indicator is tagged "Balancing" (or "Structure", "Process", "Outcome") once, in a single column, and the tag is then treated as a property of the indicator. This paper argues that the fixed-label practice misreads the concept. A balancing relationship exists between two indicators because improving one can plausibly damage the other through a shared resource, shared time, or shared attention. If that mechanism is real in one direction, it is real in the reverse direction as well. The paper therefore proposes the Reciprocity Principle of Balancing Measures, informally called Baqir's Effect: where indicator A is a credible balancing measure against indicator B, indicator B is, by the same mechanism, a credible balancing measure against A, and which of the two plays the balancing role at any moment is determined by the improvement aim, not by the indicator itself. The paper grounds the principle in the IHI definition of balancing measures, in the QI measurement literature, and in the performancemeasurement literature on unintended consequences, states plainly that no source reviewed states reciprocity as a rule, offers a three-test procedure (Mechanism, Forward, Reverse) for declaring a balancing pair, and illustrates it with a hypothetical worked example drawn from throughput-versusthoroughness indicators common in hospital registers.

title: Pricing and Staffing Human Advice When Automated Advice Improves
affiliations: Oklahoma State University

detail.title: Pricing and Staffing Human Advice When Automated Advice Improves

detail.abstract: A common view holds that as automated advice improves, human advice will move upmarket and become a deep, expensive service for wealthy clients. We study how a firm that offers both an automated tier and an advisor-assisted tier should set prices, advisor time per client, and advisor headcount as the quality of automation rises. In our model the automated tier elicits a client's objectives with limited precision, and advisor time adds precision at a decreasing rate. We show that the firm's problem in the premium has an exact solution in 𝑂(𝑛 log 𝑛) operations on a sample of 𝑛 clients, and we use it to solve the model on 25,539 respondents in the 2024 National Financial Capability Study. As automation improves, the human tier does move toward clients with the largest financial stakes, yet advisor time per client and the human premium fall rather than rise, and advisor headcount falls with them. A benchmark with a constant generalized failure rate of willingness to pay predicts the opposite. Part of the reversal comes from a term that two-option pricing rules omit. Because some clients who decline the human service leave the market instead of staying with the automated tier, the firm keeps the human service cheap. Switching this term off cuts the response of advisor time and of the premium by between a half and two thirds, depending on the route used. Competition among automated providers removes the term and raises the human premium by about 30 percent, without restoring the benchmark. Introducing automation raises consumer surplus by about a third while cutting the share of clients who receive human advice by about half.

detail.abstract: Urban water utilities face conflicting objectives: recovering fixed costs, enforcing resource conservation, and maintaining equity under climate-driven weather volatility. Using household billing records matched with satellite-derived vegetation indices in Austin, Texas, I estimate residential demand under increasing block pricing via a discrete-continuous choice model. Counterfactual Ramsey-style pricing reveals that price alone cannot resolve these trade-offs during droughts: conservation constraints generate an average welfare loss of $74 monthly for low-income households due to the prevalence of high-volume users across all income tiers. Complementary lawnzeroscaping policies offset this burden, improving distributional equity where price mechanisms fail.

detail.abstract: A bookkeeper asks an agent for a reconciliation tool; a developer asks one to change a billing system. Each must accept a day's work and show it holds. By October 2026 lawyers were setting tasks for the same agents too. In about 400,000 sessions, vendor-verified success on code-producing work was 34% for programming occupations and 29% for others, though occupation is not education. No career ladder says what someone building through agents can be trusted to deliver. I propose a measure in place of a title. The verified delegation horizon is the largest coherent piece of work, in reference hours of a qualified specialist, that a person regularly hands to agents and accepts after an independent check the agents did not see. Amplification gain, accepted reference hours per hour of attention, is a verified throughput, not a causal estimate of speedup. Both are scored per domain, Hour to Quarter; a desk pre-pilot corrected one threshold. Three large employers tried token counts and dropped them in 2026: a ranking removed, a leaderboard gamed, a budget spent. Checked work is harder to game by spending; the remaining routes have proposed, untested defences. A dated map records rival names (builder, agent manager, principal and others) without choosing. Background neutrality is the hypothesis that at an equal horizon a programming education stops predicting checked quality. The credential crossover point is the moment, domain by domain, when products of people without an IT education begin to overtake those of programmers under the same checks, after which degrees and seniority labels lose weight. Forty-one dated predictions, priced on 9 October 2026 at the median of three blind model forecasts, are registered on OSF and scored yearly until 2031; a study never run counts as a failure, and overtaking in one's own domain stands at 0.35.

title: Shaping the Menu: Information Design under Screening
affiliations: European University Institute - Economics Department (ECO)

detail.title: Shaping the Menu: Information Design under Screening

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: During the course of this research, I received financial support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under project number 504870592, which I gratefully acknowledge.

detail.abstract: How should consumers learn when a seller chooses a menu of product qualities and prices? We study information design when the seller observes the learning policy, but not consumers' private signals, before choosing its menu. Under cost-curvature conditions, we characterize optimal learning when consumer surplus receives greater weight than profit. Even with two valuations, every optimal posterior distribution combines an interval of posterior types with an efficiently served atom at the highest valuation. The induced menu features a continuum of differentiated products. Strikingly, optimal learning can also induce a lower posterior atom, separated from this interval by a support gap. Buyers in this atom either purchase an isolated low-quality product or are excluded, even when trade with every buyer creates gains. Both configurations can be optimal for the same prior and welfare weight. Served buyers with distinct posterior types are never bunched at the same quality. General finite priors can yield several separating regions and trading atoms. We also characterize the optimal joint design of learning and valuation-dependent segmentation, showing, among other results, that every posterior type with positive gains from trade must be served. Joint design can raise both consumer surplus and profit relative to buyer-optimal private learning alone. Even random assignment to segments with different learning policies and separate menus can give consumers more surplus than any single market yielding the same profit. Additional price discrimination can therefore benefit consumers, even when privacy restrictions require segmentation to reveal nothing about valuations to the seller.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

It did not involve direct recruitment of human participants or the collection of new personal financial data. Formal ethics approval and informed consent were not applicable to the reported analysis.

detail.abstract: Real-time financial transaction platforms must balance transaction integrity, availability, identity assurance, and fraud prevention. This study presents an evidence-informed event-driven reference architecture and empirically evaluates its fraud-scoring component using the PaySim synthetic mobile-money dataset. The dataset contains 6,362,620 transactions and 8,213 fraud labels (0.129%). A chronological split assigned steps 1-594 to training, 595-631 to validation, and 632-743 to the held-out test set. A class-weighted LightGBM classifier used transaction step, amount, and transaction type; account identifiers, balance variables, and the dataset's existing flagged-fraud field were excluded to reduce leakage risk. On 89,466 held-out transactions, the model achieved ROC-AUC 0.907 and average precision 0.320. At a threshold selected to maximize validation F1, test precision was 0.442, recall was 0.293, and F1 was 0.352. At a threshold of 0.5, recall increased to 0.842 while precision fell to 0.054, demonstrating the operating trade-off under class imbalance. These findings provide a reproducible benchmark for the fraud-scoring component, while the distributed architecture's end-to-end latency, throughput, and fault tolerance remain unmeasured. The paper integrates identity controls, bounded fraud decisioning, durable event publication, idempotent processing, reconciliation, and observability, and identifies further experiments required before production claims can be made.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the evolving intersection of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and the financial sector. It explores how machine learning models' transparency and interpretability shape decision-making processes in areas such as credit scoring, risk assessment, and market prediction. While conventional AI methods often function as opaque black boxes, XAI offers a solution to promote model accountability, fairness, and trust, which are critical factors in highly regulated and risk-sensitive financial environments. Drawing on 90 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science, this research applies both co-word analysis and BERTopic modeling to uncover major research themes and semantic structures within the relevant literature. The co-word network reveals distinct thematic clusters related to explainable credit risk models, interpretability in financial forecasting, and the integration of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into AI-driven financial analysis. Meanwhile, topic modeling uncovers additional topics, including SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Modelagnostic Explanations (LIME)-based explainability techniques, human-AI collaboration in decision-making, and explainable deep learning for asset pricing and sovereign risk analysis. A temporal analysis of publication trends indicates increasing scholarly attention to transparency in AI in the wake of regulatory pressure and ethical considerations in finance. The findings point to a growing emphasis on embedding interpretability into AI models to support fairness, regulatory compliance, and better-informed financial judgments. This study contributes to both academic discourse and practical application by offering a detailed map of current XAI research in finance and identifying key directions for future inquiry and technological development.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents STEPA (Structural Trajectory Embedding Predictive Architecture), a predictive representation-learning architecture designed to investigate the early detection of structural fragility in securities issuers. The proposal starts from a change of perspective: rather than assessing organizations only through states observed at isolated points in time, it represents their evolution as a trajectory in a representation space and seeks persistent changes in that dynamic.

The central hypothesis is that information distributed across regulatory filings and other public disclosures can constitute longitudinal observations of an organizational system. Represented jointly over time, these observations may reveal structural changes that are not necessarily identifiable from a single indicator, a point-in-time risk classification, or a purely distributional shift.

STEPA is grounded in predictive representation learning and takes the individual issuer's trajectory as the unit of analysis. Formally, a sequence of states z_t is organized into a trajectory τ_t whose divergence from a contextual set of reference trajectories R is assessed over time. The signal of interest is not a point deviation but the persistence of that divergence and its possible precedence relative to an external fragility event, dated independently by the experimental protocol.

The paper establishes operational definitions for observation, state, trajectory, fragility event, event date, reference set, divergence, and persistence, so that the hypothesis is falsifiable and free of circularity and look-ahead. It adds a pre-specified validation protocol with fixed parameters, baselines, primary and secondary metrics, and inference procedures for a small number of events. The public formulation describes the learning objective and the structure of the problem; it does not disclose the specific loss function, computational architecture, derived variables, weights, or proprietary training procedures. StructureWatch is the application of STEPA to regulatory intelligence for issuers. The paper presents the architecture, its foundations, the experimental design, and preliminary operational evidence, but does not report final lead-time results, which depend on completing the temporal validation.
